title: Chiefs Get Blunt Signal From Tyreek Hill After Tyquan Thornton Hurt
description: Wide receiver Tyreek Hill sent a strong, yet concise, message to the Kansas City Chiefs soon after Tyquan Thornton's ankle injury. The post Chiefs Get Blunt Signal From Tyreek Hill After Tyquan Thornton Hurt appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Tyreek Hill wasted little time sending a message to the Kansas City Chiefs and the rest of the NFL universe via social media following the severe ankle injury wide receiver Tyquan Thornton suffered in Week 4.

Hill, who reignited rumors about a potential reunion with the Chiefs roughly one week ago when posting "I think I'm ready for some cold weather" to X, was even more concise on Sunday, October 4 — yet somehow also clearer.

Hill's one-word, two-letter message reads like a direct signal to Kansas City, which the Chiefs have already answered in kind.

Mike Silver of The Athletic reported on Sunday evening that Kansas City is seriously interested in Hill, which makes it seem like only a matter of time before the two sides link up.

"Several high-ranking organizational sources confirmed Sunday night that they are very interested in signing free-agent receiver Tyreek Hill, who starred in Kansas City from 2016 to 2021," Silver wrote. "Hill suffered a gruesome knee injury almost exactly a year ago while playing for the Miami Dolphins and was released in February. He's attempting to recover from a knee dislocation and multiple torn ligaments, including an ACL, and is believed to be targeting a November return."

A silver lining exists in the timing of Thornton's injury, as it came just ahead of the Chiefs' bye in Week 5. The team will not play again until it hosts the Los Angeles Chargers on October 18, which means just two games remain on Kansas City's schedule before a showdown with the Broncos in Denver on November 1.

Silver added that Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, tight end Travis Kelce and defensive tackle Chris Jones are all on board with bringing Hill back into the fold after the team's 4-0 start.

All three were teammates with the wide receiver when the Chiefs captured the Super Bowl following the 2019-20 season.

"That's out of my hands, but I know I'd love to have 'The Cheetah' back in this building," Kelce told Silver. "He's a brother. He's one of those people who, when he sets his mind to something, he usually delivers."

Mahomes said that "it'd be pretty cool" if Hill, now 32 years old, returned to Kansas City where he began what will probably end as a Hall of Fame career.

Jones had just four words for Silver with regards to the Chiefs bringing Hill back in some capacity this season.

title: Liverpool set their eyes on 'amazing' Premier League star
description: The transfer window may be shut at the moment but, that doesn't mean the rumour mill has stopped turning. Liverpool have spent over £600 million on new players in two years and, it still feels like t...
fullText:
The transfer window may be shut at the moment but, that doesn't mean the rumour mill has stopped turning.

Liverpool have spent over £600 million on new players in two years and, it still feels like they need to improve certain areas of their squad.

At the moment, the Reds' midfield feels like their worst area on the pitch, especially now that Curtis Jones has exited.

Of course, Trey Nyoni has done a fairly decent job when called upon but, since he's still so young, he can't be playing two 90 minute matches every week.

So, this has led fans to demand new players and, even though midfield is clearly the area that Liverpool need to improve the most, their recruitment team seemingly doesn't think so.

That is, especially after the latest transfer news to emerge from Anfield.

Liverpool's defence was given a decent upgrade in the summer.

Jeremy Jacquet and Ronald Araujo were brought in with Kostas Tsimikas also making a return.

And, while Tsimikas is obviously a bit of a downgrade from Andy Robertson, the other two have helped shore Liverpool's defence up massively.

But, with so many of Liverpool's players still having their futures undecided with all of their contracts set to expire in June 2027, it's clear to see why so much change is being discussed.

At the moment, their defence doesn't need any new players but, since Joe Gomez, Tsimikas and Virgil van Dijk's contracts all expire in June, the depth among their back line could be cut in half.

This would obviously be far from ideal which is why the latest report from Football Insider about Liverpool's potential deal for Murillo should be something that excites fans.

"Liverpool and Chelsea have joined the race to sign Nottingham Forest star Murillo in 2027, sources have told Football Insider," they wrote.

"The 24-year-old has long been admired by the Premier League's top clubs, and there is a growing feeling they could move to lure him away from the City Ground after the turn of the year.

"Liverpool are seeking a long-term replacement for Virgil van Dijk, while Chelsea remain determined to bolster their squads, and both clubs could be ready to spend big.

"While his performances have attracted high-profile interest, and both Liverpool and Chelsea are keeping tabs on his situation, it will be a difficult deal to pull off."

Although one of Liverpool's main problems at the moment is the lack of homegrown players among their ranks, there aren't all that many players for them to sign.

Of course, your usual suspects such as Adam Wharton and Alex Scott have been linked with Liverpool but, if they want to get back to their best and start challenging for trophies again, they're going to need to add some top-level talent to their ranks.

Murillo, who has been described as an "excellent" player in the past would be perfect.

He's a tad older than Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni but, he already has an abundance of Premier League experience under his belt.

The Brazilian also plays in a back three under Oliver Glasner so, no matter which side he's used on, he'll be able to meet expectations.

title: Guilford County Schools responds to Grimsley marching band being kicked out of game
description: HENRICO, Va. (WGHP) — Guilford County Schools has released a statement after the Grimsley High School marching band was kicked out of a high school football game on Friday. Grimsley’s marching band was asked to leave and escorted out of the stadium during the second half after the public address announcer repeatedly warned Grimsley not […]
fullText:
HENRICO, Va. (WGHP) — Guilford County Schools has released a statement after the Grimsley High School marching band was kicked out of a high school football game on Friday.

Grimsley's marching band was asked to leave and escorted out of the stadium during the second half after the public address announcer repeatedly warned Grimsley not to play music while the ball was in play during the Whirlies' 24-17 win over Varina High School.

PREVIOUS: Grimsley marching band kicked out of high school football game

Guilford County Schools released the following statement on the controversy:

"Guilford County Schools is aware of the decision by officials at Varina High School to direct law enforcement to escort the Grimsley High School band out of the stadium.

"We understand that both schools' bands played at various times during Friday night's game and that concerns were raised regarding when bands are permitted to play according to Virginia's athletic league rules. We respect the responsibility of host administrators to enforce applicable rules and expectations consistently for all participants.

"We are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the decision and will work through the appropriate channels to address any outstanding concerns."

According to an affiliate with the Grimsley band, who wished to remain anonymous, the Varina marching band was playing while the ball was in play during the first half of the game.

At halftime, Grimsley's band leadership consulted with the head referee, who told them he would not penalize either band for playing while the ball was in play.

According to the Grimsley source, after playing music while the ball was in play twice in the second half, the public address announcer warned Grimsley again. Varina's band was not playing at the time since they were on a break after the halftime show.

Grimsley ignored these requests and kept playing while the ball was in play, which led to Varina officials ejecting the Grimsley band from the stadium with a police escort.

title: October heat wave bakes California and breaks several temperature records
description:
More than 35 million people are under heat alerts on Sunday afternoon as a dangerous multi-day October heat wave continues across nearly all of California.
Temperatures are expected to soar up to 20 degrees above normal for this time of year, into the 90s and 100s, from Northern California, including the San Francisco Bay Area, to the Mexico border.
Anadolu via Getty Images - PHOTO: People flock to Baker Beach near the Golden Gate Bridge as a heat advisory is issued in San Francisco, California, October 3, 2026. 
In some areas of California, especially urban areas, warm nights will provide little to no relief.
Los Angeles and San Diego remain under an extreme heat warning, with heat advisories posted on Sunday for San Francisco and Sacramento.
fullText:
Meanwhile, flood watches are in effect along the Gulf Coast and in Florida.

More than 35 million people are under heat alerts on Sunday afternoon as a dangerous multi-day October heat wave continues across nearly all of California.

Temperatures are expected to soar up to 20 degrees above normal for this time of year, into the 90s and 100s, from Northern California, including the San Francisco Bay Area, to the Mexico border.

In some areas of California, especially urban areas, warm nights will provide little to no relief.

Los Angeles and San Diego remain under an extreme heat warning, with heat advisories posted on Sunday for San Francisco and Sacramento.

Temperatures Sunday afternoon once again soared into the 90s across much of California, with some areas surpassing 100 degrees.

High temperatures on Sunday afternoon will be near 104 in downtown Los Angeles, 103 in Bakersfield, and will climb well into the 90s in San Diego and Sacramento.

The extreme heat warnings in Southern California will remain in effect until 8 p.m. local time on Thursday.

The heat will expand over much of the West over the next 24 hours, with temperatures running well above average for early October across a large part of the region.

Highs on Monday will reach the upper 80s as far north as southern Idaho and Montana, challenging daily record highs in Boise and Billings.

It will also be heating up in Denver on Monday, with afternoon temperatures in the upper 80s, potentially challenging a daily record high as well.

On Saturday, at least eight Southern California cities broke daily high-temperature marks, including Anaheim and San Diego, which both reached 105 degrees, and Santa Ana, which hit 107 degrees.

Meanwhile, Vista, Calif., north of San Diego, reached a high temperature of 108, breaking a daily temperature record and tying an all-time record high set on June 30, 1985.

Flood watches remain in effect from southeastern Louisiana to southern Georgia, including New Orleans; Mobile, Alabama; Tallahassee, Florida; and Brunswick, Georgia.

There is a level 2 of 4 risk on Sunday afternoon for excessive rainfall and flash flooding from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida panhandle and up into South Carolina.

Torrential rain could also trigger potentially significant flash flooding across portions of South Texas on Sunday afternoon and into the evening.

The biggest rainfall totals will occur along portions of the northern Gulf Coast, the Florida Panhandle, and from Mobile, Ala., and Biloxi, Miss., to Pensacola and Panama City, Fla., and Brownsville, Texas. In these areas, 2 to 6 inches of rain is forecast, with localized totals of 8-10 inches possible.

title: Immigration, AR-15 bans and climate lawsuits land before the Supreme Court
description:
Immigration, gun rights and climate change are on the Supreme Court docket (Stefani Reynolds)
The US Supreme Court opens its new term on Monday with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, gun rights and the fate of climate change lawsuits on the docket.
The session opens one month ahead of a crucial midterm vote that could see President Donald Trump's Republican Party lose its majority in the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate.
Losing control of Congress would force the president to have to rely even more on the conservative-dominated top court to push through his policies.
Not that it has always been in lockstep with Trump.
Trump suffered stinging defeats this year over his tariffs and bid to restrict birthright citizenship, sparking tirades by the president against the court, particularly the three justices he appointed during his first White House term.
fullText:
The US Supreme Court opens its new term on Monday with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, gun rights and the fate of climate change lawsuits on the docket.

The session opens one month ahead of a crucial midterm vote that could see President Donald Trump's Republican Party lose its majority in the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate.

Losing control of Congress would force the president to have to rely even more on the conservative-dominated top court to push through his policies.

Not that it has always been in lockstep with Trump.

Trump suffered stinging defeats this year over his tariffs and bid to restrict birthright citizenship, sparking tirades by the president against the court, particularly the three justices he appointed during his first White House term.

"I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often," he told Time magazine in a recent interview.

At the same time, the 6-3 conservative majority has allowed Trump to vastly expand his executive powers and handed him a number of victories on what is known as the emergency docket, where cases are fast-tracked without oral arguments.

At the end of September, for example, in an immigration case in which the three liberal justices dissented, the court allowed the administration to continue for the time being to deport undocumented migrants to countries that are not their own.

The court will hear oral arguments in that case during the fall term and a ruling in the administration's favor could open the floodgates to more so-called "third country" deportations.

More than 25,000 people have been sent to third countries since Trump returned to office after reaching secret agreements with some 35 nations, most of them in Latin America and Africa.

- 'Concerned about the future' -

In another immigration case, the court will weigh a new practice of automatically detaining undocumented migrants -- even those who have lived in the United States for years -- instead of releasing them while their cases are being adjudicated.

"The Trump administration is interpreting that mandatory detention statute in a way that no administration has ever done in the 30 years since that statute was enacted," said Cecillia Wang, the national legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). "It's to pressure people to, as the government puts it, self-deport."

The opening case of the term may decide whether climate suits brought by local governments against oil companies for their role in global warming can proceed or whether federal law should prevail.

On the election front, the Supreme Court will take up an Arizona law requiring proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

Trump and fellow Republicans have baselessly claimed for years that many non-citizens vote in US elections but studies have shown the actual number is insignificant.

Gun ownership returns to the court in a case challenging state or local bans on certain semi-automatic weapons such as AR-15s.

The role of religion in public education will be tested when the justices hear a case involving a Catholic preschool in Colorado that denies admission to children of LGBTQ+ parents.

The question in the case is "whether they have a right to receive taxpayer dollars without following the non-discrimination rules that apply to everyone else," said Dan Mack, director of the ACLU's Program on Freedom of Religion and Belief.

On the eve of the new term, Justice Samuel Alito, a staunch conservative, gave a rare public interview in which he told Fox News Sunday he was "concerned about the future of the court."

"There has been a concerted effort to intimidate the court and justices on the court to try to influence us to decide cases," the 76-year-old Alito said.

A recent Gallup survey found that Americans' views of the Supreme Court are at their least positive since the organization began polling on the institution in 1972.

Only 34 percent of US adults approve of the job the court is doing, essentially unchanged from the record-low 33 percent approval tallied in July, Gallup said.

title: U.S. monitoring suspected fatal pneumonic plague case in Russia, official says
description:
The State Department is monitoring reports of a suspected fatal pneumonic plague case in Russia and is urging Moscow to share accurate information quickly as details remain unconfirmed.
A State Department official told Fox News that the U.S. is aware of reports of a death in Irkutsk Oblast, a region in southeastern Siberia, and is watching the situation closely with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other federal agencies. The official stressed that many details have not been confirmed and called on Russian authorities to reveal what they know.
fullText:
The State Department is monitoring reports of a suspected fatal pneumonic plague case in Russia and is urging Moscow to share accurate information quickly as details remain unconfirmed.

A State Department official told Fox News that the U.S. is aware of reports of a death in Irkutsk Oblast, a region in southeastern Siberia, and is watching the situation closely with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other federal agencies. The official stressed that many details have not been confirmed and called on Russian authorities to reveal what they know.

Former CIA officer Dan Hoffman told Fox News Digital that the U.S. intelligence community is likely to be collecting all-source intelligence on the incident.

SCIENTISTS CRACK THE CODE ON NEW VACCINE FOR DEADLY PLAGUE BACTERIA

"I would also expect our embassy in Moscow to be engaging with their diplomatic counterparts at an official level because we might have people in Russia who might be at risk," Hoffman warned.

"Washington will be speaking to all of our allies and partners in the region and sharing what we know."

DEADLY BACTERIA THAT DOOMED NAPOLEON'S ARMY DISCOVERED 213 YEARS AFTER RUSSIAN RETREAT

Pneumonic plague can be treated with common antibiotics, especially when treatment begins early, the official said. Appropriate therapy should begin as soon as plague is suspected, and patients can be treated with intravenous or oral antimicrobials depending on the severity of illness and other factors, according to the CDC.

Cases of pneumonic plague occur naturally in many parts of the world, according to the State Department official.

The official said the safety and security of U.S. citizens remains the department’s top priority and encouraged Americans traveling overseas to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, or STEP, to receive updates.

title: Former Prince Andrew takes legal action over warrants used in Epstein-related arrest
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor photographed leaving a police station in February...
fullText:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest in February.

The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are challenging the search warrants used in Sandringham and at Royal Lodge in Windsor relating to his arrest, as first reported by the Telegraph.

Thames Valley Police confirmed: "We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court."

"As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further," a spokesperson for the force that carried out the arrest said.

Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.

A court hearing will be held on Thursday afternoon to begin considering this bid to quash the warrants, with the hearing set to begin in private. The judge will initially hear a request by the police to keep some documents private.

The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor had been arrested - and the legal challenge is against the chief constable of Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court.

"Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service.

Vamos said such disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search.

"The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos.

It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said.

For several days after the arrest, police were seen searching Mountbatten-Windsor's property at Marsh Farm in Sandringham and at his former home, Royal Lodge, on the Windsor estate.

The arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice.

They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy.

Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said those links had been severed.

After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February he was taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation.

The launch of this legal action against the police over the search warrants is the first public pushback from the former prince, who has lost his home, titles and public status, with charities and businesses distancing themselves from him.

Thames Valley Police says its investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is continuing.

In a previous update it said the force had been "working with the United States Department of Justice to get further information that may be related to this investigation".

Detectives also highlighted that allegations of sexual misconduct could be considered as part of this inquiry into potential misconduct in public office.

Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing in his associations with Epstein.

title: Own a smartphone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down | Chi Onwurah
description: A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use...
fullText:
A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them

Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee

Debates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.

As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.

But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to 30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.

Developers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple and Google to protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.

Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, as reported in the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per year to Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.

My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found that Apple and Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.

Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.

Its consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.

But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.

This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.

Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee

fullText:
Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model

Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.

It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon.

Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.

Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.

Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.

Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)

Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing

Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS

Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)

Dimensions: 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm

The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.

The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.

The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.

The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.

Siri AI, as the new system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.

It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.

The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability.

It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.

The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.

That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.

The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.

The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.

But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.

The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.

Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.

The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.

The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).

For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air costs £1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359.

The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.

The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.

The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.

All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.

Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.

Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

title: Internet Watch Foundation reports huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material

fullText:
Abuse material monitor says number of AI images assessed this year is already 40% higher than last year’s total

AI-generated child sexual abuse material is proliferating online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.

Analysts at the Internet Watch Foundation have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the prior year. The UK-based IWF, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.

Instances of AI-made child sexual abuse material have been rising for several years, with a huge surge in videos in particular, although the latest IWF figures refer to still images only. The majority of the images seen by analysts were of girls, and of children aged seven to 13.

The IWF said the figures underlined the need for new statutory regulation on AI.

Andy Burnham’s government has not signalled that a new bill focused on the technology is imminent. Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, has said “nothing is off the table” in terms of fresh regulation, but that the test for any legislative proposal will be: “Will it make the British people safer?”

Hannah Swirsky, the head of policy at the IWF, said she backed calls from parliamentarians for “binding legislation on AI” to compel companies to build safer models. “It is incumbent on tech companies to build tools which cannot be abused this way,” she said. This problem has been created by technology, and if companies won’t build tools which are safe by design.”

AI-generated child sexual abuse material is illegal in the UK and the government has also made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others. Developing a model designed to produce hyper-realistic child sexual abuse material carries a criminal sentence of up to five years.

A government spokesperson said: “UK law is clear that child sexual abuse material is illegal, regardless of whether it is AI-generated or not. We are going further by banning AI models that are used to create this type of abuse material and produce sickening, hyper-realistic imagery that often contains the likeness of real children.”

AI has also enabled online predators to create explicit images of children. The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, has received 420 reports from children concerning images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.

The use of AI tools to create abuse tools has led to the National Crime Agency and IWF encouraging parents and guardians to keep pictures of their children off social media. The guidance suggests making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.

title: How perfect storm has rained on Derby's parade
description: BBC Sport looks at how Turki Alalshikh's aborted takeover of Derby County has contributed to a poor start to their Championship season.
fullText:
It was supposed to be a new dawn at Derby.

Instead, the Rams have been left to pick up the pieces after the last-minute collapse of Turki Alalshikh's takeover on the eve of the season.

This month, Mo Fuseini's last-gasp goal rescued a point at Burnley which stopped Derby going into the international break bottom of the Championship.

Yet they have just five points from their opening eight games and remain in the relegation zone.

So what impact has the aborted takeover had at Pride Park and what can head coach John Eustace do to salvage the season?

This season was supposed to be the one when the Rams pushed for promotion.

When Eustace took over in February 2025, Derby were fourth-from-bottom in the Championship and questions were asked why he swapped a promotion challenge with Blackburn, who were fifth, for a relegation scrap.

Internal difficulties and restrictions at Ewood Park played a part but Eustace was sold a long-term plan which was survival, consolidation and then challenging for a top-flight return.

Yet this term's promotion assault was significantly hindered when Alalshikh pulled out of his planned takeover an hour before the deal was due to be completed in August, leaving Derby scrambling after a summer of work.

The collapse blindsided the club and transfer plans were affected despite owner David Clowes remaining committed to bankrolling the Rams.

Derby chief executive Stephen Pearce has denied the summer disruption impacted recruitment but it is undeniable plans suffered.

"From a transfer perspective we hadn't lost anything we wanted to do," he told BBC Radio Derby.

Eustace admitted, though, they had to understandably review targets following the takeover collapse.

"Obviously, we had our targets that we were looking at and who we wanted to bring in," he told the Derby Telegraph this month.

"When the takeover eventually didn't happen, we've lost a lot of momentum on players that we were looking at."

Eustace wanted Liam Millar only for Birmingham City to sign the Hull City forward on loan for the season and Derby moved for Fuseini - who was due to join Blues before they signed Millar - from Union Saint-Gilloise on deadline day.

Ben Brereton-Diaz scored eight goals in 41 games for Derby on loan last season but the Rams' situation meant they could not move quick enough to bring him back and, by the time they did, the Southampton forward had committed to going to Sheffield United.

Birmingham winger Patrick Roberts was another on the list but the 29-year-old's wages were a stumbling block.

None of the players on loan last season had options to buy meaning the Rams needed to renegotiate for those who returned, with Bobby Clark costing £6m from Red Bull Salzburg as the club were left open to market forces this summer.

That did at least help them re-sign midfielder David Ozoh for £4m on deadline day, when Crystal Palace valued him at £10m at the start of August.

Clark, Ozoh and Sammie Szmodics - who has already hit the requirements to make his £2.7m move from Ipswich permanent - were influential last term but their returns only ensure the squad has returned to the same level as last season, rather than significantly improving it.

Pisa striker Henrik Meister, who has scored just twice in a year, joined on loan and was seen as a good back-up to Carlton Morris and Patrick Agyemang but the 22-year-old Dane has needed to lead the line with that duo injured.

He then suffered a head injury against Birmingham this month while Agyemang has been out since April with a serious Achilles problem.

Injuries have formed part of the problems at Pride Park with reigning player of the season Matt Clarke unlikely to be back before December.

Goalkeeper Jacob Widell Zetterstrom is also out for six weeks while Brighton loanee Eiran Cashin is sidelined and Derry Murkin, expected to be the Rams' first-choice left-back, is out until after Christmas.

It all means Eustace has been unable to field the same back four in successive games since August.

The head coach and Derby have been unlucky, with Eustace especially left powerless and having to continue to firefight 20 months after joining.

There was a clear intention not to be in the same position as this time last year, with a promotion challenge expected - and Derby resisted interest for players including Agyemang and Zetterstrom - but it is a frustrating mirror image.

With eighth place now enough for a play-off spot, it was viewed as an achievable target this year. Instead, their season is, so far, following a similar path after eight points from the opening 10 games of last term.

Yet last season, their form from the final 36 games - if averaged across the whole campaign - would have been enough to finish fifth rather than ending eighth, four points adrift of the top six.

It is proof Derby - who host Wrexham on Saturday - and Eustace can succeed despite their current position, but only adds to the frustration of another slow start.

His job is not under threat and it is recognised the former Rams midfielder is the best man to steer them away from trouble, with a track record to prove it.

He was sacked by Birmingham when they were sixth in 2023, with Blues going on to be relegated after appointing Wayne Rooney as his successor, while he saved Blackburn from the drop in 2023-24 before leaving them in the play-off places.

But, after the perfect storm which has enveloped Pride Park, Eustace needs the pieces to fall into place again.

title: Irwin could ride at Brands Hatch after hospital discharge
description: Northern Ireland's Glenn Irwin is discharged from hospital after crashing in Sunday's British Superbike round at Donington Park.
fullText:
Northern Ireland's Glenn Irwin has been discharged from hospital after crashing in Sunday's British Superbike round at Donington Park.

The 36-year-old was moved to Queen's Medical Centre in Nottingham after the incident because of "concern regarding a possible spinal fracture".

However, there was a positive update from the British Superbike Championship.

It said that Irwin been "pronounced clear and discharged and will be reviewed for fitness to ride at Brands Hatch".

Irwin crashed on the penultimate lap of the third BSB race of the weekend at Starkey's Bridge.

He was assessed and treated at the medial centre at the circuit, and was conscious and stable throughout.

It is the second time that the Ducati rider has been taken to hospital after a crash this season.

Irwin sustained pelvic and neck injuries in a crash at Snetterton in July and missed the two remaining races that weekend.

BSB leader Kyle Ryde won the opening two races of the weekend at Donington but Scott Redding clinched the third and final outing to take the championship to the final weekend at Brands Hatch from 17-18 October.

title: Metcalfe back in Wales WXV reckoning for Japan
description: Nel Metcalfe is in a 30-strong party that will be led by co-captains Alex Callender and Kate Williams for back-to-back Tests in Japan.
fullText:
Full-back Nel Metcalfe has a chance to resurrect her Wales career after being named in Sean Lynn's squad for their WXV double-header against Japan.

The 21-year-old Gloucester-Hartpury player has fully recovered from the knee injury that ruled her out of the 2026 Women's Six Nations.

Lynn named Metcalfe in his extended training squad for the stunning WXV win against South Africa and subsequent defeat by the United States, but she did not make the matchday squads.

Uncapped props Stella Orrin and Crystal James also make the cut in a 30-strong party that will be led by flankers and co-captains Alex Callender and Kate Williams.

But Jaz and Alisha Joyce have not made the squad while wing Seren Singleton, who played her part as Wales beat South Africa, is also omitted.

Lynn remaining positive despite Wales' USA setback

'Lions Women can learn from darts and 1997'

Metcalfe's recovery included facing Barbarians for Wales in June in an uncapped encounter.

After making their debuts in September, wing Amy Williams, prop Elan Jones and hooker Shanelle Williams will also travel to Japan.

Wales will face the hosts at Prince Chichibu Memorial Stadium, Tokyo on Saturday, 24 October (10:30 BST) followed by their second meeting at Kumagaya Rugby Stadium, Saitama Prefecture seven days later (07:00 GMT).

Lynn said: "This was a tough selection process after our performances against South Africa and USA, we asked the players to move the dial, and we did that in those two Test matches.

"We scored eight tries against South Africa and the disappointment of the players with the two-point deficit against USA, a team ranked sixth in the world, demonstrated the shift in mindset we need.

"All the hard work the players, coaches and staff put in across pre-season was there for all to see and we laid some real foundations in how we want to play and the team's identity.

"We know we have a long way to go before we become the team, we want to be but the tour to play the Sakura XV in Japan is an exciting challenge for us all."

title: How Keith Alexander blazed a trail for black football managers
description: Ex-players and family members on the legacy of the late Lincoln, Peterborough and Macclesfield boss.
fullText:
When Keith Alexander died in 2010, he was honoured up and down the country, including on one of football's biggest stages as England players donned black armbands for a match at Wembley.

It was a fitting tribute to a man who was not only an admired and respected figure in the game, but a trailblazer who helped pave the way for more black managers in English professional football.

As part of Black History Month, those who knew him best have been reflecting on his lasting impact.

"Keith remains a beacon of hope for us all, and I know his story continues to inspire us," says Leon Mann, a co-founder of the Football Black List, external, which gives out an award in his memory.

"When we see a number of black British or black managers in the Premier League, we should pause and remember Keith's contribution, because it would have played its part, one hundred per cent."

Although he was not the first permanent black manager in the Football League – Tony Collins took the reins at Rochdale in 1960 – Alexander helped inspire a new generation to follow in his footsteps after spells in charge of Lincoln City, Peterborough United and Macclesfield, among others.

Born in Nottingham in 1956 to St Lucian parents, Alexander was proud of his English upbringing and Caribbean heritage, his sons Matt and Paul say.

Alexander spoke openly about the racism he encountered as a player, which included monkey chants and bananas being thrown at him.

"He experienced loads of it, especially in his early days," Matt says. "There was loads of racism and throwing bananas, that kind of stuff.

"I'd be really surprised if you spoke to any black footballer of that generation who hadn't experienced the same sort of thing."

Despite this, Paul says race was rarely discussed at home.

"It was never a conversation about how difficult it was for black youths growing up.

"It was, you will be successful at what you do and you work hard for what you want."

However, he adds: "I think he was conscious he did have to work twice as hard."

After a long playing career, Alexander took charge of Lincoln City in 1993. After a season in charge, he went on to manage non-league Ilkeston Town and Northwich Victoria.

In 2002, he was named Lincoln boss for a second spell and, working with a tight budget, helped guide the club from the depths of administration to the League Two play-off places in four successive seasons.

Former striker Franny Green says Alexander will always be remembered for "bringing players from non-league and giving them an opportunity".

"If you go through Lincoln's history, Keith's name is going to be one of the biggest when it comes to what he did."

Green recalls having a real affinity with Alexander. "I think it helped because of my race and Keith's race," he adds.

Recalling the first time he met Alexander during a trial at Ilkeston, Green says: "I was 16, this tall slim kid with a mini afro and he was just really charming towards me.

"He said just go and play football – there's no pressure."

Simon Weaver joined Lincoln City in the summer of 2002 after previously playing under Alexander at Ilkeston.

He recalls his former boss's great ability to unite a dressing room.

One moment that sticks in his memory is the first time he was invited for a training session at Ilkeston.

"I played quite well in training – afterwards I went and knocked on his [office] and he was sat there with his feet up and a bunch of grapes."

Weaver was asked to "just come and play" for the team on Saturday.

"He was just so relaxed," he recalls. "He just made me feel at ease, saying just come and do you what you did [in training].

"We played away first game and won – I got a black eye and I'm thinking, 'I'm liking this, this is my cup of tea'."

Alexander was managing Macclesfield when he died in 2010 after falling ill after a game. He was 53.

Tributes poured in from across football, with clubs across the country observing a minute's silence.

At the time, his son Paul described him as "a very humble man", adding: "He didn't realise the impact he had on others just by walking into a room."

In recent years, players who have received the Keith Alexander Award from the Football Black List have included Yaya Toure, Shaka Hislop and Kerry Davis, the first black woman to play for the England women's national team.

His legacy also lives on through the Sacred Sports Foundation, which he founded in St Lucia to help young people through sport.

Mann says Alexander will be remembered for the opportunities he created for others and his willingness to challenge racism in football – and that should never be forgotten.

CORRECTION, 5 October 2026: An earlier version of this article suggested Alexander died after falling ill at a game. He actually fell ill at home after the game.

title: Connor out, Lewis in as England name World Cup squad
description: Leeds Rhinos half-back Jake Connor is left out of England's Rugby League World Cup squad, with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis beating him to a place.
fullText:
Jake Connor missed out on a Rugby League World Cup spot by a "small margin" as England seek the players who can best stick to their gameplan, head coach Brian McDermott says.

Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor, the 2025 Super League Man of Steel, was left out of the 23-man squad for the tournament - to be held largely in Australia - with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis making the cut instead.

For Connor, it is another England disappointment to follow his controversial omission from the squad for last autumn's home series against Australia.

"Jake Connor missed out on selection by a small margin and it came down to who I think can best stick to the game plan and attack plan," McDermott said.

The 31-year-old had been expected to make the squad after being talked up by McDermott and enjoying a strong domestic season.

But Hull KR's Lewis, who endured an inconsistent year, has done enough to convince McDermott that he should join captain George Williams, the Warrington stand-off, and Wigan's Harry Smith as half-back options.

England begin their World Cup campaign against Tonga in Perth on 17 October, before facing France in the same city on 24 October and then Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on 30 October.

England squad: Matty Ashton (Warrington Wolves), AJ Brimson (Gold Coast Titans), Ben Currie (Warrington Wolves), Zach Eckersley (Wigan Warriors), Herbie Farnworth (Dolphins), Ethan Havard (Wigan Warriors), Max King (Bulldogs), Morgan Knowles (Dolphins), Mikey Lewis (Hull KR), Jez Litten (Hull KR), Junior Nsemba (Wigan Warriors), Brad O'Neill (Wigan Warriors), Kai Pearce-Paul (Wests Tigers), Victor Radley (Sydney Roosters), Hugo Savala (Sydney Roosters), Harry Smith (Wigan Warriors), Morgan Smithies (Canberra Raiders), Luke Thompson (Wigan Warriors), Sam Walters (Wigan Warriors), Ben Talty (Brisbane Broncos), Jack Welsby (St Helens), George Williams (Warrington Wolves), Dom Young (Newcastle Knights)

Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad

Hawkins among five World Cup winners in England squad

There has been much debate about which half-backs would make the England squad after McDermott said last month that he would probably take three to the World Cup, and that captain Williams - who is heading to Australia to join NRL club Dolphins after the tournament - would be one of them.

McDermott said: "Jake has had a really good year. He had an outstanding year last year and got Man of Steel.

"What I've got is a squad full of players who I believe will best play to the game style, the attack plan or game model we identified many weeks ago, that I think we need to compete with the leading nations.

"We can't do the usual things, and I made this a point when I took the job. We've got to play with a point of difference.

"I've got a squad here who I believe are best suited to the attack plan and game model I think England need to play."

Explaining his decision to select Lewis, McDermott added: "I've picked a group of player that have recent history of playing in finals, winning finals, delivering when it matters.

"Mikey Lewis won a World Club Challenge at the start of this year and guided his team to a Challenge Cup final.

"I get he wasn't in the best of shape towards the back of the year and incurred a couple of bans but again, I'll just point people to the attack plan and game model I think England need to have to compete with the leading nations."

When he replaced Shaun Wane as head coach, McDermott indicated that he was keen to use heritage players - those who qualify for England through family background - to ensure the strongest possible squad.

He has called up two uncapped Australia-born players - versatile back Hugo Savala, part of Sydney Roosters' NRL Grand Final-winning squad, and Brisbane Broncos' front-rower Ben Talty.

Bulldogs prop Max King, born in Huddersfield while his Australian father David was a player there, also earns a first call-up. Victor Radley and AJ Brimson complete the Australia-born contingent in the squad.

Grand Final winners Wakefield have no players in the squad, with Tom Johnstone, Mike McMeeken, Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Jake Trueman all needing time to recover from injuries.

"It's a real shame that the Wakefield boys aren't available," McDermott said. "There's nothing we or they can do. They're all booked in for operations at the end of the year."

And also injured were Sydney Roosters centre Billy Smith - a scorer in Sunday's NRL Grand Final - Wigan centre Jake Wardle, Leeds winger Ash Handley and prop Mikolaj Oledzki, who is leaving Headingley to join NRL side Perth Bears.

Grand Finalists Warrington have three players in the squad - Matty Ashton and Ben Currie joining captain Williams - while Wigan have seven, including Man of Steel winner Brad O'Neill and uncapped centre Zach Eckersley.

Mikey Lewis over Jake Connor feels like a call made based on pace rather than any other metric, as the Hull KR half is much more of a runner than his opposite number.

He's also perhaps more of an off-the-bench spark than the Leeds playmaker, given George Williams and Harry Smith's blend of run threat and game management will probably get the nod at six and seven.

Herbie Farnworth has been one of the best players in the world for some time and has taken his game to new levels in 2026, and getting the centre involved must be among Brian McDermott's biggest tactical challenges.

Dom Young is another thoroughbred who England will look to out wide, having helped Newcastle to the NRL Grand Final.

Victor Radley's influence and savage tackling makes him a shoo-in for the pack, something that was missed in last year's Ashes series against Australia, and there are other big hitters in the ranks with Morgan Knowles and Morgan Smithies also sharpened by their NRL exploits, and Brad O'Neill back in the international picture after a Man of Steel year.

Staying with the pack, the prospect of a Kai Pearce-Paul and Junior Nsemba second-row pairing whets the appetite.

Elsewhere, the new imports from the NRL have pedigree; Max King has played State of Origin, Hugo Savala can jump into a number of backs spots and Ben Talty is an athletic front-rower who helped Brisbane to success in 2025.

Zach Eckersley has impressed for Wigan this year, and his strong build and athleticism - coupled with an ability to put a winger away - make him a solid inclusion, while Matty Ashton's return after his missed the Ashes with an anterior cruciate knee ligament injury gives England genuine pace out wide.

Everyone will have their opinion on the squad, which features no selections from Super League champions Wakefield - albeit with some contenders unavailable - but there is a balance to the selection.

McDermott has said England might need something different to truly test the best, and it is that conundrum which will again be at the forefront of his thoughts.

Reece Walsh has secured a place in Australia's men's World Cup squad, also named on Monday - although head coach Kevin Walters has refused to confirm whether he will be first-choice full-back.

Walsh has struggled to hit the heights of last season, when he inspired Brisbane Broncos to their first NRL Grand Final triumph in 19 years before helping Australia to a 3-0 Test series win over England.

He missed the end of this season to have ankle surgery, but with Penrith's Dylan Edwards ruled out of the World Cup with a knee injury, Walsh will vie for the full-back spot with James Tedesco - man of the match as Sydney Roosters beat Newcastle Knights 19-18 in Sunday's NRL Grand Final.

Loose forward Isaah Yeo will delay surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to captain Australia.

Winger Mark Nawaqanitawase - who scored two tries in Sydney's win on Sunday - is not in the squad because of his impending code switch to union with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights. Second-row forward Angus Crichton is absent for the same reason, as he is joining NSW Waratahs.

Star half-back Nathan Cleary is out of the tournament with a broken ankle.

Australia men's squad: Isaah Yeo (captain), Bradman Best, Jack Bostock, Blake Brailey, Pat Carrigan, Lindsay Collins, Reuben Cotter, Tom Dearden, Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, David Fifita, Harry Grant, Keaon Koloamatangi, Liam Martin, Latrell Mitchell, Mitchell Moses, Cameron Munster, Cameron Murray, Jacob Preston, Kotoni Staggs, James Tedesco, Tom Trbojevic, Sam Walker, Reece Walsh.

Dual-code winger Nawaqanitawase stars as Roosters win NRL Final

Ali Brigginshaw has missed out on the chance to go for a fourth World Cup winners' medal after being omitted from Australia's women's squad.

Head coach Jess Skinner said the 36-year-old Brisbane half-back - Australia's captain when they won the tournament in Manchester four years ago - was "upset" to be left out.

"That was one of the hardest phone calls I've had to make as a coach to a player and to talk about her and where she was," Skinner said.

Australia women's squad: Isabelle Kelly (captain), Tarryn Aiken, Kezie Apps, Shaylee Bent, Jaime Chapman, Abbi Church, Quincy Dodd, Millie Elliott, Tiana Penitani Gray, Olivia Higgins, Ellie Johnston, Keilee Joseph, Jocelyn Kelleher, Olivia Kernick, Keeley Nizza, Sariah Paki, Julia Robinson, Jessica Sergis, Jesse Southwell, Simaima Taufa, Sarah Togatuki, Tamika Upton, Makenzie Weale.

title: The only side in Nations League yet to concede? Northern Ireland
description: With three clean sheets from three games in Uefa Nations League Group B2, Northern Ireland are the only team in this year's competition yet to concede a goal.
fullText:
Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One NI, BBC Three, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary available online.

When Switzerland equalised in the 11th minute of their eventual 2-1 win over Slovenia on Saturday, there was just one team left in the 2026-27 Uefa Nations League yet to concede a goal - Northern Ireland.

Michael O'Neill's side have kept three consecutive clean sheets upon their return to the second tier of the competition, beating Georgia and Ukraine to nil with a scoreless stalemate against Hungary in between during this window.

Indeed, across this campaign and the 2024-25 edition when Northern Ireland played in League C, they have kept seven clean sheets in their past nine Nations League games, conceding just three goals in the process.

Should they manage to keep Georgia out again in Belfast on Monday night, it will be the side's longest run of clean sheets in nine years.

They did live somewhat dangerously in the reverse fixture in Tbilisi, with goalkeeper Pierce Charles saving a penalty from Paris St-Germain forward Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in a player of the match performance.

Despite the absence of Daniel Ballard and Conor Bradley through injury, the Queens Park Rangers loanee has had precious little to do in the two games since, however.

Hungary had their only shot on target in injury time at Windsor Park last week, while the side's record goalscorer David Healy described the stopper's two saves in the 3-0 victory against Ukraine as "ones for the camera".

"I think the clean sheets are a real plus for us and we want to maintain that because history tells us that Northern Ireland are never the highest scoring team," said O'Neill.

"If you look at the xG [Expected Goals] in the games, people have different opinions on that, but the xG for the opposition has been low and that means we've got a good defensive structure.

"It means our young defenders are coping with the game at this level, but it also means that we defend well as a team and the best teams do that."

NI team will 'have bumps along the road' - O'Neill

Who has 'no ceiling' as Northern Ireland shine in Nations League?

'Different' Morrison gives NI new option

Always evident in an effective O'Neill team is a desire to work hard off the ball. If Isaac Price, who scored his 11th international goal against Ukraine, is the closest thing the side have to a flair player, the West Bromwich Albion attacker still covers plenty of ground going the other way.

"You watch PSG, and their willingness to defend and to run, is a great example," added O'Neill.

"We have that ability to run when we lose the ball. We've got great recovery runners in our team, and that's a big reason why teams have found it difficult against us."

Already in this extended international window, O'Neill has talked of what he perceives as a "snobbery" about his team's style of play.

Comments made by then Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann last October were branded "disrespectful" by former Northern Ireland defender Stephen Craigan at the time, while opposition managers have frequently used words such as direct or physical in the months since.

Against Ukraine on Friday, Northern Ireland had 27.2% possession, according to Opta the lowest recorded in Nations League history for a win by more than one goal.

"We see some of the best teams play with very little possession as well. Sometimes you have teams who have a lot of possession but struggle to do anything with it," said O'Neill.

"You can control the game without the ball as much as with the ball."

Northern Ireland's long-ball statistics can be skewed somewhat by the fact that goalkeeper Pierce Charles possesses such a fantastic range of passing, and O'Neill cited his side's second goal against Ukraine as an example of the football his side can play.

"The quality of our play shouldn't be underestimated," he said.

"Our second goal against Ukraine, that's as good a goal as you'll see. The number of passes and how we worked the ball the full length of the pitch, the cross and the header.

"If you said 'would you love 60% possession?' then of course we would, but at this minute in time, that's an area to improve on.

"People have opinions, but really the only opinion that counts to me is that of the players and the belief that the players have."

On the evidence of recent results, that is no area of concern and Northern Ireland's defensive solidity is not just confined to the Nations League.

In all competitions they have kept eight clean sheets from their past 10 games at home and on Monday night Georgia will look to become the first visitors to Belfast to score more than once since Cyprus in June 2022.

"I think over the last three or four years, we've played the same system and I think boys are getting more comfortable and they understand their jobs," said Sunderland defender Trai Hume.

"That's not just the starting XI, it's the boys that come into the team who understand what they have to do too. On and off the ball you understand where you have to be on the pitch and, when you understand that, it makes the game a lot easier.

"Once you understand your role in the system, that's when you can start to express yourself and I think you're starting to see that."

title: £117m Rogers failed at Bournemouth - and feared he may not make it
description: A look at the point in club-record £117m Chelsea signing Morgan Rogers' career when he doubted whether he could make it at the highest level.
fullText:
Three years before becoming Chelsea's £117m club-record signing, Morgan Rogers watched his value fall to just £1m and questioned whether he would make it at all.

For Rogers, the transition from academy football to the men's game was not as seamless as he had hoped and, in his own words, it took a series of "difficult loans" for him to break through.

Bournemouth, who Chelsea face at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, were the first of two underwhelming Championship loan spells for Rogers, alongside a later stint at Blackpool, while he was a Manchester City player.

It was a setback for a player who had been a regular England youth international and one of West Bromwich Albion's brightest academy prospects.

In a recent interview with Chelsea's club channel, Rogers said that period taught him how to "take knocks".

Asked what his rise through the EFL had taught him, he replied: "Everything."

After a long pause, he added: "I needed that next challenge, to be taken out of my comfort zone and find the player I was going to be in professional football.

"I think the academy player I was, if you watch me then, is not the same player I am now. I am a completely different player. I had to learn that on loan.

"The one thing I learned when going through these difficult loans is that I couldn't care less what people say about me. I just care about what I can control."

"I don't think there's such a thing as a bad loan," Rogers' first loan manager at Lincoln City, Michael Appleton, told BBC Sport.

Appleton had worked in West Brom's academy and knew Rogers was one of the most highly rated prospects there. He made it his mission to bring him to Sincil Bank in League One.

He remembers Rogers having a big personality and speaking up in team meetings despite arriving as an 18-year-old. The forward went on to score six goals and provide two assists in 28 appearances after joining shortly after lockdown.

En route to the play-off final, which Lincoln lost to Blackpool, Appleton recalls one moment in particular.

"We played Portsmouth away and they had three or four absolute units in the team," he added. "We were setting up for set-pieces and almost running out of players to pick up these giants.

"Without any hesitation whatsoever, Morgan said: 'Make me a marker. I'll head the ball out of our box.'

"This was a teenager on his first loan.

"He was full of confidence because he was playing well, but he took the defensive side of the game just as seriously as trying to impact the opposition's box. For me, that's a great example of him as a person and as a player."

However, after earning an opportunity in the Championship with Bournemouth, Rogers started only three matches and scored once under then-manager Scott Parker, whose side secured promotion back to the Premier League.

Rogers had little impact and was described as a "slow burner" by former scout Des Taylor, who brought him in.

He added: "You could see his ability having scouted him at Lincoln, but it wasn't clear what he would become. We saw his Lincoln loan spell turn him from a boy into a man.

"He showed he could handle the physical side of things after coming from Man City's academy. Unfortunately, we signed him late in the window. We saw him as a number 10, but Parker was not really playing with a number 10.

"I don't think it was a great time for him because he wasn't getting game time and, when he did, it wasn't in the position he wanted. He was a victim of the transition. It was no fault of Scott's, but it didn't work out."

Former Bournemouth team-mate Steve Cook added: "Bournemouth had the opportunity to sign him permanently (reportedly for £9m) but it didn't work out.

"He didn't let it stop him. First and foremost, he was a really good lad. He was energetic away from the football pitch and I think that character has helped take him to where he is now.

"He's a great example that not every journey is straightforward. You need setbacks to make you hungry and appreciate what you've got. He worked hard, listened, had a willingness to learn and wanted to prove people wrong."

Rogers' loan spell was cut short and he returned to academy football before an injury delayed his next move to Blackpool until the following January.

The move reunited Rogers with Appleton in the Championship, but the manager was sacked after only two weeks and replaced by Mick McCarthy.

Rogers made 20 appearances, both as a starter and substitute, scoring once as the Tangerines were relegated to League One after appointing a third manager in April.

"Unfortunately, he played one game against Watford and then I got sacked. That wasn't great for either of us," Appleton added.

"He'd been patient, I'd been patient while he recovered from his summer injury, we'd finally reconnected and then I was out of the building.

"I don't think he played as much as he would have liked after that, but he dealt with it professionally and in the right way."

Rogers says this period was "difficult" and tried not to compare himself to former team-mates who overtook him and got opportunities before him.

He even doubted whether he would make it but said his family and friends kept him grounded.

Notably, his "best friend in football", Cole Palmer, joined Chelsea for £42.5m having not needed a loan move to establish himself at Manchester City. At the same time, Rogers joined Middlesbrough for just £1m.

A run of five goals and three assists during Middlesbrough's six-game run to the Carabao Cup semi-finals alerted Aston Villa, where several of Rogers' former West Brom coaches were working in senior academy roles, to make an initial £8m move in the winter window.

"Morgan is a great example that careers aren't always a straight line," Appleton explained.

From a £9m prospect to a £1m gamble and eventually a £117m Chelsea signing, his story is a reminder that some of the best footballers need to overcome setbacks from a young age.
