title: How Evans defied history to become Britain's first world rally champion in 25 years
description: Elfyn Evans has been the nearly-man of world rally until he finally emulated the feats of Colin McRae and Richard Burns.
fullText:
For what must have felt like an eternity, Elfyn Evans feared history was repeating itself yet again.

At 3.05pm local time in Sardinia on Sunday, Evans could only stand and watch as another world rally title looked to be slipping from his grasp.

Evans was preparing in his head yet another runners-up speech - it would be his sixth - as he waited for Oliver Solberg to cross the finish line and be crowned world champion.

How could this be happening again?

Of the five previous times he had been championship runner-up, three had been decided on the final day and twice after he had taken a lead into the final event.

But at 3.06pm, for once the motor-racing gods were on his side.

With just two turns to go on the final stage of the final round and with victory in sight, Solberg somehow careered off the track into the Sardinian sand to hand Evans his first world title.

In the most dramatic of finishes, the 37-year-old from north Wales became the first British winner of the World Rally Championship (WRC) in 25 years.

Only two British men had taken the title since the WRC's 1977 inception, matching the exploits of legendary pair Colin McRae (1995) and Richard Burns (2001).

Louise Aitken-Walker was Britain's first world champion when WRC ran a women's version in 1990.

As it happened: Evans wins title as Solberg crashes on final stage

The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory

"It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done," said Evans.

"It's been a difficult weekend. I felt on Friday things were slipping away. We were a bit powerless with the road position we had and Oliver was flying."

His experienced co-driver Scott Martin revealed Evans was already apologising for his stage performance as they waited for Solberg to finish.

"I've said all week that until we arrived at the beach after that last stage it was never over. How true that turned out to be," said Martin.

Evans and Martin have been consistent performers throughout the 2026 championship, through the streets of Monaco, the ice and snow of Sweden, the flowing roads of Chile, and the punishing, sun-baked gravel tracks of southern Europe.

Despite winning only two of the previous 12 events, the pair took a 21-point lead into the final race at Rally Italia Sardegna.

Solberg, whose father Petter won the 2003 title, was around one kilometre from glory only to suffer motorsport's version of Devon Loch.

"The lead up to this event gave us a bit of a buffer and we just about managed to hold on at the end. It was an incredible finish," said Evans.

"I feel for [Solberg] after he came so close and lost at the last moment. I've been in a similar situation and it will be tough for him for a few days, but he's shown he's one to watch for the future."

Evans, like Solberg, is also from fine rally-driving stock. His father Gwyndaf was British champion, as well as runner-up four times, but the motor dealer from farming stock never got the break to be a major contender on the world stage.

The curse of finishing second passed down to his son who had already turned professional by the time his father claimed the last of those near misses in 2010.

Evans clinched his first WRC stage win in Germany in 2014 and a first podium in Argentina a year later, before having to drop down to the WRC2 class in 2016.

Evans admitted that blow only fueled his determination to make it in the WRC and a first rally victory followed - in his home event in Wales - in 2017.

He has been remarkably consistent, finishing second for the title in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 and, perhaps most agonisingly, to Sebastien Ogier by just four points in the final race of 2025.

He appeared condemned to be one of sport's great runners-up until the late drama of Sardinia threw up one of the championship's most thrilling finishes.

There may have been a stroke of fortune about the title win, but few can deny Evans earned it.

title: A nation divided as Ronaldo left with big decision on Portugal future
description: BBC Sport looks at what could be the end of Cristiano Ronaldo's international career just days before the expected fanfare of Lionel Messi's Argentina goodbye.
fullText:
As Lionel Messi prepares to get a hero's farewell for his successful international career, Cristiano Ronaldo's could have ended with him running down the tunnel at the final whistle of a game he did not play.

After the World Cup, Argentina's Messi, 39, decided to retire from international football, while Ronaldo, 41, opted to play on for Portugal.

Yet there is the possibility that Messi's Argentina career will end up lasting a few days longer - with a home friendly with Benin on Tuesday marked as his final game.

Ronaldo, furious at being made to warm up and not be brought on against Norway in the Nations League, walked out on the Portugal squad after finding out he would not start against Denmark either.

The Al-Nassr forward has scored 146 goals and won 234 caps for Portugal - both world records.

After such a high-profile falling-out with new boss Jorge Jesus, also a larger than life character who does not back down, Ronaldo is facing a big decision.

Jesus has insisted he would be welcome back if he wants to return and talks between Ronaldo, his representatives and the Portuguese FA are ongoing as they look for a solution.

While Ronaldo could not carry on playing forever, this is not how he would have expected his international career to end.

His fans are remaining loyal to him, with social media full of posts supporting Ronaldo and criticising Jesus, while on the other side some fans and a lot of Portugal's media have been critical of what they see as selfish behaviour.

Ahead of Portugal's next match against Denmark in November lies a big decision for one of the world's greatest ever players.

Is this the end for Ronaldo - and would Portugal miss him?

It has all happened very quickly.

After the World Cup, Portugal replaced Roberto Martinez with Jesus, who had been Ronaldo's boss with Al-Nassr last season.

Less than two weeks ago, Ronaldo said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want."

Things were still looking OK when he started in the 1-0 win over Wales.

Jesus told Ronaldo he would be on the bench for the next game against Norway. After being told to warm up for a period of the game, he remained an unused substitute in a Portugal game for the first time in 18 years.

Guillem Balague, who wrote a book about Ronaldo in 2015, said: "He gets asked to warm up for the whole of the second half, practically.

"There are tacit rules in football: you don't do that to Pele, to Diego Maradona, to Lionel Messi, to Cristiano, right? That's what he's seen, that you don't do that to those kind of players."

And as the final whistle went he went down the tunnel instead of going to the fans with his team-mates.

Jesus said there was no falling out - but confirmed Ronaldo would not start the next game with Denmark either.

At that point Ronaldo left the training camp - and wrote on social media: "In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated."

Portugal's FA president Pedro Proenca flew to Copenhagen, landing at 02:30 in the morning, to try to smooth things over with Ronaldo but failed.

He has since said: "He is in the national team on sporting merit, and that must be unquestionable. We have to pay tribute to Ronaldo."

After beating Norway on Sunday in their final Nations League match - again without Ronaldo - Jesus said: "If he wants to, he'll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who's going to decide.

"He's the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team."

On several billboards in Lisbon posters went up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.

They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain.

"Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."

One was placed next to the Estadio da Luz, home of Benfica - who Jesus managed to three league titles.

At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.

Denmark striker Rasmus Hojlund, incidentally, celebrated his goal with his idol Ronaldo's trademark 'siuuu' - something he has done previously when netting against Portugal.

Portugal's newspapers had differing perspectives.

Record - who the forward owns shares in - said "Ronaldo leaves after clash with Jesus" and Jornal de Noticias said it was "the end of a historic era".

"A sad goodbye," said Bola, while Jogo went for "CR7 turns his back on the national team".

Meanwhile, videos were posted online of angry fans ripping up their Portugal jerseys.

Jesus and Proenca were booed leaving a building in Copenhagen.

But many foreign fans purely supported Portugal because of Ronaldo - so they do not necessarily represent the views of actual Portuguese supporters.

Portugal fan Maria Ribeiro, from Lisbon, said: "It is so hard for all us fans. We all love him but it is getting too much now. It is hard to imagine Portugal without Ronaldo but maybe this is the time. There is too much arguing between ourselves."

Ronaldo's World Cup career ends in tears as 'pandering' Martinez departs

Ronaldo's search for a record 1,000 career goals remains on but will he have to finish that at club level in Saudi Arabia?

He has scored 979 times for Portugal, Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al-Nassr.

While his old rival Messi scored eight goals, and assisted four more, to take Argentina to the summer World Cup final - Portugal fell at the last-16 stage.

Ronaldo scored three goals in the tournament but failed to have an impact in their loss to Spain, leading BBC pundit Chris Sutton to say he was "waddling around the pitch like a grandad".

Ronaldo's former United team-mate Wayne Rooney added: "He is a genius, a superstar. What he has given to football and millions of people is something very rare.

"He will be disappointed because he believed he could win this tournament. But time gets us all. It's a sad day for football."

In the last nine years of Ronaldo's international career, Portugal's win percentage without him is slightly better - 64% to 63% - and they have scored 2.7 goals a game without him compared to 2.1 with him.

The two biggest wins in their history - 9-0 over Luxembourg and 9-1 against Armenia - came in the last two qualifying matches that he missed, both through suspension.

Journalist Marcus Alves, who covers Portugal, said: "How much gratitude is enough? That's a question that Portuguese fans have been asking for a few years now.

"The whole soap opera that seems to follow the mere presence of the 41-year-old striker got to a point where patience was running out.

"Of Portugal's last five coaches, Ronaldo had issues with four of them – Carlos Queiroz, Paulo Bento, Fernando Santos and now Jesus. That's too much distraction when Portugal have arguably their best generation ever."

Ronaldo 'greatest symbol' of Portugal - Fernandes

Portugal boss says door open for Ronaldo return

title: London City gelling, Man City flying - takeaways from WSL start
description: After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season.
fullText:
After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season.

Here are five key takeaways from the opening weeks.

For the first time this decade, the established order of the WSL looks under threat.

London City Lionesses and Tottenham have been bullish about climbing the table, while Liverpool also sought to kick on this season.

After five games, London City look the most convincing, with Sunday's statement 6-1 win at Spurs a dazzling example of the talent and depth manager Eder Maestre has at his disposal.

Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas headlined some eye-catching summer signings and she scored twice against Tottenham.

But it was the manner in which the whole team dismantled their previously impressive opponents that was so spectacular, with fellow forwards Kadidiatou Diani and Danielle van de Donk also looking a class above.

"This kind of win can be a game-changer," Maestre said.

No doubt. It is the kind of display that can lead to talk of a title charge.

For Spurs, a humiliating home loss is a reality check after promising early results.

Liverpool acquitted themselves well in narrow losses away to both Manchester clubs but, with key attacking players such as Vivien Endemann missing against United, they lacked creativity.

That points to perhaps the biggest thing both Liverpool and Spurs lack in comparison with London City: squad depth.

Five wins from five with 16 goals scored, defending champions Manchester City have picked up where they left off.

Sunday's comeback victory over Arsenal made it City's best start to a season since opening the 2017-18 campaign with seven straight victories, cementing their status as the team to beat.

In so doing, City also likely ended the Gunners' title aspirations even this early on.

It helps when their best players are performing. Khadija Shaw's contract renewal in the summer was key and the striker has five league goals already. England winger Lauren Hemp is also in fine form, contributing four goals and two assists.

After some quietly shrewd additions in Beth Mead, Carlotta Wamser and Niamh Charles, City look well set once again.

Their closest rivals are Chelsea, who have responded to an opening-day draw against Aston Villa by winning four straight games without conceding a goal.

While boss Sonia Bompastor wants them to be more clinical, their defensive strength is something they have over City.

As for Arsenal, the gap is 10 points to leaders City, and strong pre-season hopes of a first league title since 2018-19 are vanishing, with manager Renee Slegers conceding on Sunday: "At the moment, we are not in the conversation."

Manchester United's summer of upheaval bled into the start of the season, with Eva Olid's arrival from Hearts beginning with convincing defeats by London City and Chelsea.

The message from the club was that this would be a season of transition but recent performances suggest they are getting to grips with her style of play.

Saturday's 1-0 win over Liverpool was United's fourth straight victory in all competitions, with 18 goals scored in the process.

"I am so happy for the players - they deserve it," Olid said. "We have started to click in a lot of things and they fight for each other.

"But there is still a lot to improve. We created chances, but our last pass and our finishing needs to be better."

Summer signing Andrea Medina has been a huge positive on the left wing, with her contribution to the team more pronounced than a single goal suggests.

A trip to bottom side Charlton after the break is a presentable chance for more points before a stern test against Manchester City the following weekend.

This season is the WSL's biggest ever, literally, with the league expanding from 12 to 14 teams and three coming up from WSL 2.

Crystal Palace look the most comfortable of the promoted sides, boasting six points from five games and they moved to eighth in the WSL table by drawing at Aston Villa on Sunday.

But things are more difficult for the other promoted sides, Birmingham and Charlton, who prop up the table.

Despite some promising patches, WSL 2 champions Birmingham have just two points and one of those came against Crystal Palace.

At least France forward Oceane Hurtre looks suited to this level, sitting as joint top scorer in the WSL with five goals from five games.

Hurtre scored against Everton in defeat on Sunday but defender Neve Herron summed things up by saying Blues were "second to everything" after the game.

Meanwhile, it looks bleak for Charlton, bottom of the table with zero points, 15 goals against and only two goals scored.

After their 5-1 loss to Brighton on Sunday, goalkeeper and captain Sophie Whitehouse said: "It just wasn't good enough.

"It's a tough league. The jump up is so big. You can't make any mistakes."

Finally, it is too soon to draw conclusions but attendances at some of the league's biggest matches have been down on previous seasons.

For instance, Chelsea hosted Arsenal on 27 September in a fervent atmosphere, but the game had 36% fewer in Stamford Bridge than in January this year.

Similarly, Liverpool against Everton at Anfield was 19% down on last season, albeit the Merseyside derby was the first game of the 2025-26 season.

Three Saturdays ago, Arsenal kicked off against Manchester United at 17:30 in front of 29,853 fans. Last season, it was a lunchtime fixture that welcomed 37,627.

For balance, it ought to be highlighted that the Manchester City v Arsenal game on Sunday was promoted from the Joie Stadium to Etihad Stadium, and definitely had more than the 4,300 who attended the game last season.

Official figures have yet to be released for it.

Nevertheless, while this is a small sample size, paying customers is a potential trend to monitor as the WSL wrestles with the continued challenge of the schedule.

title: Salty celebrations, questionable signings and Test bolters - Prem talking points
description: Bristol set out their top-four aspirations with a statement win, while Gloucester's renaissance continues in the second round of Prem action.
fullText:
The stats piled up after a car-crash performance by Harlequins in a 48-0 shellacking by Gloucester.

The biggest league defeat in 26 years. Seventeen penalties conceded. Only two entries made into the opposition 22m. Not one of their starting forward pack making more than four carries.

It was a desperately under-powered display.

Boss Jason Gilmore described it as "totally unacceptable" in the aftermath.

The Australian has overseen a few eyesores during his time in charge; a 38-0 reverse at Sandy Park and a 40-14 reverse at the club's festive fixture at Allianz Stadium come to mind.

Gilmore says turning around the tanker will take time. Contracts have to run down and money reassigned to different areas of the squad.

Full-back George Furbank was this summer's big investment. The 29-year-old marked his Prem debut for his new club with a couple of trademark breaks, slicing up from backfield.

He is a classy addition, but is he the signing they needed, with little room to manoeuvre under the salary cap and a creaking forward pack limiting the supply of ball to the backline?

England loosehead prop Fin Baxter has been out for 10 months with a foot injury, but should be back soon. South African tighthead Sampie Swiegers is in contention for selection after his arrival in London.

Chandler Cunningham-South and Guido Petti may be due a run from the start.

But, with Alex Dombrandt expected to miss the majority of the season with a knee ligament injury sustained in June, Quins will need them all to hit the ground running.

Snarl up front, rather than style out back, is where they are lacking.

Gloucester thrash sorry Quins to go top of the Prem

Bristol chief executive Tom Tainton caught some flak earlier this year for saying the Bears needs to think like a marketing agency, rather than a traditional rugby club,, external to grow its fanbase.

The image of Louis Rees-Zammit mimicking Northampton star Henry Pollock's 'pulse-check' celebration, and the delight it sparked among fans, were evidence in his favour however.

A 20,756-strong crowd at Ashton Gate – up 5,000 on their win in the same fixture last year, partly helped by football's international break – relished a spiky performance all round from Rees-Zammit.

The Wales international could easily have had a hat-trick in a 34-26 win over Saints, but was body-checked by Tommy Freeman in pursuit of a final-play chip ahead, earning a penalty try and sending his opposite number on his way with a few blunt observations.

Rees-Zammit, restored to the wing after dabbling at full-back on his return from American football, has four tries already this season and Bristol, who were well in last year's play-off hunt before a dip in form after the Six Nations, are looking ominous.

The next four rounds of action – Saracens (a), Exeter (h), Leicester (h) and Bath (a) – are a big chance to dent some other top-four hopefuls.

Rees-Zammit was not the only wing on a wind-up this weekend either, by the way. Adam Radwan's gleeful celebration of his try for Leicester against former club Newcastle, marking his territory by pointing to the pitch below his studs, drew jeers from the Kingston Park crowd.

Rees-Zammit stars as Bristol power past Northampton

England boss Steve Borthwick was at The Rec on Friday night.

He will have taken particular interest in one 28th-minute scrum.

Beno Obano and Will Stuart, either side of hooker Tom Dunn, made the Exeter front row look as though they were wearing skis rather than studs, sending the visitors skidding backwards at a rate of knots.

Considering Baxter's lack of game time and Bevan Rodd being ruled out of the autumn after wrist surgery, Obano may well be the back-up loosehead option to Ellis Genge for England's Nations Championship campaign.

Stuart's welcome return from an Achilles injury is likely to have him installed as the tighthead replacement behind the excellent Joe Heyes.

Borthwick may well lean into their Bath connection as he rebuilds a 'bomb squad' bench which was crucial to England's good form in 2025.

Gloucester fly-half Charlie Atkinson may well be twisting Borthwick's arm as well.

The 25-year-old has been central to the Cherry and Whites' electric start to the season.

He set up the opening try of their thrashing of Harlequins with a cute jink past Will Porter and then a pinpoint crossfield bomb for Ben Loader a couple of passages later. A hint of a dummy and a dart took Atkinson himself over for his team's fourth.

His substandard goal-kicking may count against him. Of players with a minimum of 10 kicks at goal, only Bath's Santi Carreras had a lower success-rate off the tee in 2025-26. Team-mate George Barton had kicking duties on Saturday.

But if Borthwick wants a back-up stand-off that more closely replicates the playing style of first-choice Fin Smith, Atkinson may be due promotion after three appearances for England A last season.

Bath gain revenge on Exeter to win 11-try thriller

Last year's runners-up Exeter have begun the season with successive defeats, but there was significant improvement on their opening-day defeat by Gloucester as they threatened to climb off the canvas and overturn Bath, just as they did in June's semi-final at The Rec.

A fit, firing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso - 133m carried, nine defenders beaten and two tries - was an obvious plus for the Chiefs.

But Kane James made a major step forward.

The 21-year-old Welsh international, who only made his first Prem start at the beginning of this season, was fearless at the Rec, flying into contact with relish.

As well as that wince-inducing ball-carrying, he was cleaning up on the floor, winning three turnovers.

Australia international Tom Hooper is now back in the south west, but has had a high workload switching between Chiefs and Wallabies' duties.

James has made a decent claim to holding on to his back-row spot a little longer.

With the clock in the red and five points down on the scoreboard, Newcastle Red Bulls smuggled the ball out wide to a full-flight Christian Wade.

The 35-year-old had a corridor of space to accelerate into and 45m to cover to the tryline.

Leicester replacement Tom Whiteley just about managed to shut the gap and, a few phases later, Newcastle infringed to give away a penalty and snuff out any hope of victory.

Like Wade's try record however, it is coming for Newcastle.

After a decent showing in defeat away to champions Northampton in the opening round, Newcastle had the upper hand on Leicester for large stretches.

The visitors made more than double the number of tackles of their opponents.

The accuracy to turn possession into points is one of a number of things that will surely improve steeply as the Newcastle squad, revamped with more than 20 summer signings, gel together.

Leicester hold off Newcastle for first Prem win

title: Bournemouth unhappy after Scott injured with England
description: Bournemouth are unhappy with the way they believe England handled the injury to Alex Scott - which means he could now be out for up to eight weeks.
fullText:
Bournemouth are unhappy with the way they believe England handled the injury to midfielder Alex Scott - which means he could now be out for up to eight weeks.

Scott has withdrawn from the England squad to face the Czech Republic in the Nations League on Tuesday with a thigh injury.

He felt the issue prior to Saturday's 7-0 win over Croatia, but played 70 minutes in central midfield alongside Elliot Anderson before being substituted.

England coach Thomas Tuchel described Scott's injury as "a strange one" in his Monday news conference.

"I'm very sad about it. He trained in full before Croatia, did extra work after the training sessions, we knew he was in treatment but there were only green lights from him and the medics," said Tuchel.

"When we were aware there was slight discomfort during the match and asked if he wanted to come off he said no. After the match, he said he could have played 90 minutes and didn't feel an injury.

"Even before the scan he didn't feel injured so it's a strange one. There was zero risk taken from our side."

However, according to sources, there is frustration at Bournemouth about how England have handled their midfielder, given they knew he was nursing the thigh issue.

The 23-year-old is now set to be out for six to eight weeks with the quadriceps issue.

Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa has also been ruled out of the fixture at Wembley as a precautionary measure, with the 28-year-old to return to the Premier League champions for treatment on an injury.

Tuchel said that Konsa's issues were "nothing major but not worth the risk taking" after the centre-back first missed the match with the Czech Republic in Prague on 29 September and then sustained an injury against Croatia.

"Ezri felt discomfort when he came into camp, played with it against Spain and it got a bit worse so he stayed in camp and tried everything for the match against the Czech Republic and it came too soon," Tuchel added.

"Unfortunately, he got another hit on the quad and that caused a light trauma and we decided not to let him play through this pain, so he left camp to get treatment for both his issues now."

Scott is now likely to be absent for the nine games Bournemouth are due to play between 10 October and 8 November.

Alongside their weekend Premier League commitments, they will play on Wednesday or Thursday for four consecutive weeks, facing Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Prague in the Europa League and Aston Villa in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

Scott made his England debut in the 2-0 win over the Czech Republic, before his full debut four days later, after which Tuchel was effusive with his praise.

"First start and what a start, what a performance," said Tuchel. "He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making is at the highest level.

"He plays with so much confidence. He is so active, so confident. The work rate off the ball.

"He is just the complete package. He gave us a lot of mobility and a lot of variety and work rate in the centre of the pitch."

Scott joins French forward Eli Junior Kroupi on Bournemouth's injury list, with the 20-year-old still unavailable after sustaining a foot problem in pre-season.

The Cherries are 17th in the Premier League and are winless after five matches, drawing three times and losing twice.

Marco Rose's side defeated Lincoln to progress in the EFL Cup, and won 2-1 at La Liga side Real Sociedad on their European debut.

They return to Premier League action at Chelsea on Saturday (15:00 BST) and play Sunderland, Manchester United, Leeds and Ipswich prior to the November international break.

title: £800m in, £800m out - Why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
description: Manchester City's owners have been found guilty of injecting money into the club. At Manchester United, fans are frustrated at how much has been taken out.
fullText:
The Premier League panel's report laid it out in black and white.

"The club's income was hugely overstated by over £830 million."

In other words, Manchester City's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations over a number of years by pumping money into the club that should not have been recorded as sponsorship income.

The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.

Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.

And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m.

Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city resulted in money being ploughed in, it meant a similar significant sum being paid out in interest for the other.

United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."

This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.

Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.

Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.

In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.

To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.

Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.

When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.

Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.

Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.

In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.

While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.

Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.

When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.

Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.

It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.

In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.

Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.

The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.

Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.

In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.

When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.

The overall target is undefined, but it is pretty clear Champions League qualification will be a significant part of it.

title: F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz
description: F1 "needs to have a hard look at" itself in the wake of unprecedented software glitches that affected the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Carlos Sainz says.
fullText:
Formula 1 "needs to have a hard look at" itself in the wake of unprecedented software glitches that affected Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Williams driver Carlos Sainz says.

A bug in the software for a wet-weather engine map led to a number of cars struggling to move on formation laps before the start of the race.

The start had to be abandoned, a new software code issued, and the race eventually got under way an hour and a half later than scheduled.

Sainz, who is a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "It is clear the regulations are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units and for the manufacturers. Who decided five years ago that this was the direction to go?

"We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can.

"But clearly what was decided four or five years ago was wrong. We need to learn as a sport not to make those mistakes again."

Governing body the FIA has launched a "full review" of the situation.

It arose because there had been very little wet-weather running this year, and the specific circumstances that triggered the bug had not previously arisen.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "It's a good reminder for all of us that we should probably make sure that complexity doesn't get out of hand and that we keep things as under control as possible.

"And I'm sure we'll have discussions with the teams, with the FIA and with F1 to see how we can protect ourselves from those situations moving forward and make sure we can keep the complexity of the cars and the systems under control."

Sainz's remarks are a reference to the wider debate about this year's new engine regulations, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.

The engines are fundamentally energy starved, which has led to drivers feeling the cars behave in a counter-intuitive way, and have reduced the impact of driver skill.

The engines have about 1,000bhp on full power, but only 540bhp when the batteries run out.

Because of the way the regulations have been arranged, the batteries are fully deploying and recharging several times a lap. And a series of highly complex restrictions have been introduced relating to the operations of the engine to try to alleviate some of the issues that have arisen.

One of those is what triggered the problem in Malaysia - the total electrical power is reduced from 350kW (470bhp) to 250kW (335bhp) in the wet.

One of the idiosyncrasies of the rules is that the cars slow down at the end of straights to recharge batteries, and many challenging fast corners have been neutered because they are being used as what two-time champion Fernando Alonso has described as "charging stations for the car".

The 50-50 split was decided upon five or six years ago, and teams have been warning the FIA that these issues would arise since at least 2023.

But at no point was the 50-50 split questioned until just before the start of this year, when it became apparent how significant the impact of the engines would be.

Since the cars began to run this year, a series of rule changes have been introduced to address the issues.

This year, the total amount of recovery allowed is altered depending on how energy starved a circuit is.

The energy split will become 60-40 in favour of internal combustion in two steps by 2028.

And teams and F1 bosses are already working on finalising a new engine formula that will introduce power units that are never energy starved.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for naturally aspirated V8s with no hybrid at all.

But the current likeliest solution is a V8 turbo with somewhere in the region of 15-25% electrical power, which will mostly be used as a simple push-to-pass system.

fullText:
Even with bond yields hovering at more than 20-year highs, the stock market has barely flinched.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose Friday to sit less than 1% from its record high while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) was near an all-time high as a weak jobs report lowered expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike this year.

Up until now, elevated oil prices, AI-related risks, and deteriorating market breadth have suggested a pullback may be just around the corner.

"The market has had every reason to sell off, and it hasn't sold off yet, and to me it feels like it's running out of time," Sean McLaughlin, chief options strategist at All Star Charts, told Yahoo Finance. "The path of least resistance appears to be higher."

Seasonality also leans bullish as October, while traditionally volatile, has posted a 63% win rate over the past 20 years.

And looking at the four-year presidential cycle, the S&P 500 has posted an average return of 18.3% over the next seven months during the past 50 years, McLaughlin noted.

"We've got earnings season coming up, and if we get any glimmer of good news, I think the market is going to be caught offside, and we could have a really significant rally over the next three to six months," McLaughlin said.

That doesn't mean the market's resilience hasn't been a head-scratcher, particularly as the 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to its highest level since 2002.

Wall Street anticipates yields on the 10-year can climb higher before they begin to weigh on valuations.

"Historical data show that valuations start compressing after 5.5%, and everyone from investors to corporations to consumers would have to redo the math on their investments," Fundstrat economic strategist Hardika Singh wrote in a note last week.

UBS strategists last week noted that yields become more concerning for stocks when economic growth begins to falter. That's not the case with a booming AI build-out in the US.

"We forecast S&P 500 earnings growth of 25% this year and 14% in 2027, which should help equities absorb moderately higher interest rates," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer Americas and global head of equities at UBS, wrote.

To spread risk, Hoffmann-Burchardi recommends buying stocks across global markets such as the US, Europe, and Asia.

At the same time, she suggests targeting major growth trends such as AI, power and resources, and healthcare (XLL).

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

title: Saudi-led coalition says its jets are bombing Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels
description:
— Forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government began a major offensive Monday against the Iranian-backed Houthis rebels on the country's Red Sea coast, under an intensified air campaign by the Saudi-led coalition.
The offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region. 
The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis.
fullText:
ADEN, Yemen (AP) — Forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government began a major offensive Monday against the Iranian-backed Houthis rebels on the country's Red Sea coast, under an intensified air campaign by the Saudi-led coalition.

The offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region.

The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition has secured "air protection" of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.

The campaign and its details could not be immediately independently verified.

The Houthi rebels seized the town of Turbah on Sunday, shortly before the internationally recognized government announced a major military operation against them.

The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.

Turbah sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for the government forces defending Taiz against the Houthis.

Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts in a series of advances, paving the way for the rebels to encircle Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.

The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September. They captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial chokepoint through which 12% of global trade transits.

In their announcement Sunday, the Saudi-backed government said it was mobilizing troops across government-held areas.

Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called for the international community to provide support to his government.

Hours after al-Alimi's declaration, a Saudi military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, vowed "full operational support" to the Yemeni government forces, until the Houthis are "eliminated."

Al-Malki also stressed Saudi Arabia's right to take all necessary measures to deter the rebels who continued to fire missiles and drones at the kingdom as part of the nearly three-month escalation that revived Yemen's civil war.

On Monday, factions allied with the Saudi-backed coalition fighting the Houthis said they launched offensives against the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis had seized in their latest advances.

They attacked Houthi positions in the town of Dhubab, on the coast of Bab el-Mandeb strait, said Col. Majed al-Nazili, spokesman of the Saudi-backed forces.

The Giants Brigades, a government-allied group, said it began a "decisive military operation against the Houthi militias," also in the Bab el-Mandeb area.

Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation — dubbed "Yemen Dawn" — has started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-controlled capital, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup."

Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on Sanaa. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes by the Saudi coalition on their territories, including Sanaa.

The latest flare-up began in mid-July, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing the airport in Sanaa to prevent the landing of an unauthorized Iranian flight. The rebels responded with missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces in the country.

They also announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and attacked several Saudi-linked vessels.

Then in September, they intensified their campaign, storming down the Red Sea coast in their biggest land grab in years.

The rebels' taking of Turbah "will likely severely constrain Yemeni government-aligned forces' ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions" across Taiz province and the provincial capital of Taiz, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.

"Disrupting resupply has military value, of course, but controlling all the roads in and out of areas to the north of Turbah also prevents government forces from retreating out of the city," the think tank wrote in a Sunday analysis.

Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis descended from their northern stronghold, capturing Sanaa and forcing the government to flee into exile in Saudi Arabia. The war created one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters and killed more than 150,000 people.

The latest bout of violence has killed at least 959 people and wounded over 4,200 others, according to the World Health Organization. The flare-up forced over 145,000 people to flee their homes inside Yemen, according to the U.N. migration agency. More than 3,000 others fled across the waters into Djibouti, the agency reported.

Last week, Yemen's health ministry — part of the internationally recognized government — warned about the impact of the conflict on health facilities and medical staff across the entire Taiz province. The ministry said in a statement on Friday that health facilities in coastal, western and southern areas of the province have closed or are barely partially functioning.

title: 2 victims identified after Georgia homecoming shooting as police appeal for help
description:
Two people killed after gunfire erupted at a neighborhood homecoming party in Georgia on Sunday have been identified.
The shooting, which left another 35 injured, began at about 1:25 a.m. Sunday at a neighborhood party that spanned four blocks in the city of Vienna.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy in a press conference described it as a “senseless act of violence” and said the investigation is ongoing.
fullText:
Two people killed after gunfire erupted at a neighborhood homecoming party in Georgia on Sunday have been identified.

The shooting, which left another 35 injured, began at about 1:25 a.m. Sunday at a neighborhood party that spanned four blocks in the city of Vienna.

Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy in a press conference described it as a "senseless act of violence" and said the investigation is ongoing. No arrests have been reported.

The two victims killed have been named as Ja’Quavion Aderious Jackson, 21, and Macaleb Malik Jackson, 23.

The 35 other victims ranged in age from 14 to 51, with their conditions ranging from stable to critical, Peavy said.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation has appealed to anyone with information about the shooting to contact authorities or submit an anonymous tip as law enforcement continues to investigate.

Newsweek contacted the Georgia Bureau of Investigation for comment via email on Monday, outside of regular working hours.

Authorities estimated that around 1,000 people had been at the party at the time of the shooting.

"If you can imagine over 1,000 people, I would say, and they're going every direction. Even while we were on scene, there was still gunfire about a block away while all of us were on scene trying to get attention, medical attention to the ones that needed it," Peavy told WMAZ-TV.

It was not immediately clear how many of the injured had been shot, with victims taken to several local hospitals.

Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls, who responded to the incident, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution that two men were pronounced dead at the scene. He said dozens of people had been struck by bullets, and around a dozen others were injured while fleeing.

"This doesn’t—it’s not supposed to—happen in a small town like that. It’s something you hear on the news in bigger cities," Walls told the paper.

"And even in bigger cities, you don’t hear that kind of a number," he said, referencing the number of those injured.

The party was being held to celebrate a local high school football team’s victory at a homecoming game on Friday night, the AJC reported.

Peavy said that a number of officers had been on duty over the weekend to ensure celebrations were safe, and that Friday night had gone smoothly.

"Last night was a different story. We’re still working through the investigation to see what went wrong. But a large party with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come," he said on Sunday.

The Dooly County Sheriff's Office and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation are working together to investigate the incident. Authorities said they do not believe there is any ongoing threat to the public at this time.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick, Tobias Meyjes and Tony Phillips.

title: Tennessee prison chief had execution problems before Christa Pike, officials say
description:
Christa Gail Pike, on death row for a slaying, appears in court on April 12, 2012, to fight a conviction in a 2001 attack on an inmate. - Dipti Vaidya/USA Today Network/Imagn Images/Reuters
Before the botched execution of Christa Pike, Frank Strada reportedly had a history of overseeing execution missteps in two states.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Saturday announced Correction Commissioner Strada would step down later this month following the backlash after the attempted execution left Pike on a ventilator, unconscious in a hospital. Less than three years earlier, Lee brought Strada on to lead the Department of Correction, tasking him with reforming Tennessee’s execution system after enduring concerns over the state’s approach to the death penalty.
fullText:
Before the botched execution of Christa Pike, Frank Strada reportedly had a history of overseeing execution missteps in two states.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Saturday announced Correction Commissioner Strada would step down later this month following the backlash after the attempted execution left Pike on a ventilator, unconscious in a hospital. Less than three years earlier, Lee brought Strada on to lead the Department of Correction, tasking him with reforming Tennessee’s execution system after enduring concerns over the state’s approach to the death penalty.

But in Strada’s previous role as an official in Arizona’s prisons system, he oversaw three executions that administrators and observers raised concerns over, saying executioners flouted the state’s official policies. Now under his current supervision, Pike is the second person this year who Tennessee officials have failed to execute after problems with the IV injections.

The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment when asked by CNN about Strada’s involvement in these prior execution problems.

Pike’s debilitating survival has brought to light Strada’s history overseeing executions that didn’t follow typical protocol, and larger questions about the death penalty by both proponents and opponents. Lee has suspended executions for the year as an investigation is underway.

“The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing, so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that’s what they want to be done in their name,” Stephen Ferrell, Pike’s lawyer, told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Sunday. “This torturous execution leaves so many questions that the state of Tennessee will refuse to answer.”

As his resignation was announced, Strada said, “stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward.”

“I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary,” Strada said in a statement Saturday, “and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”

Here’s the latest on Strada’s final days overseeing Tennessee’s prisons, and what happened inside Pike’s death chamber.

On Saturday, the state Attorney General’s Office retained Ed Stanton, a former US attorney, to conduct an independent review of the Department of Correction’s actions in carrying out Pike’s execution, Gov. Lee’s office announced.

Stanton previously oversaw an independent review of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol in 2022, the governor’s office said, which resulted in the state substantially rewriting its protocol.

Strada began leading Tennessee’s correction department in 2023 when he was tasked with enacting that new protocol among other duties. An Air Force veteran, Strada was a senior official in Arizona’s prison system who previously had worked nearly 30 years for the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

In naming Strada to lead the agency, Lee said Strada’s “extensive corrections management and law enforcement experience make him well-suited to lead the Department of Correction.”

Strada served as a deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry. His tenure was marked with controversy around three executions that were performed after an eight-year moratorium in the state.

All three had issues with establishing IV lines to administer the lethal drug, lawyers said. The problems prompted Arizona’s governor to call for an independent review of execution protocols. The review in Arizona was announced weeks after Lee promoted Strada to his current post in Tennessee.

In a 2023 sworn declaration, Ryan Thornell, director of Arizona’s corrections department, said he was “unable to locate sufficient documentation” about execution procedures under the previous administration, which included Strada. He cited “several critical issues” impacting the agency’s ability to conduct executions, including inadequate expertise, efficacy of lethal injection drugs, and procedures with the IV team.

Thornell said he couldn’t find documentation identifying the pharmacist who compounded the lethal drugs. Without naming Strada, he said a prior deputy director was the main point of contact with the pharmacist but said he didn’t record anything. The effectiveness of the current supplies of the lethal drug couldn’t be guaranteed and needed to be tested to ensure safety and efficacy prior to use, Thornell said.

Meanwhile, he said the IV team who worked on the state’s most recent execution had been told by the prior administration to only use the femoral central line, which was against the department’s policy.

In Tennessee, questions have mounted around the Department of Correction’s protocol around executions, including IV administration to administer lethal doses.

Pike’s case wasn’t the first time state officials had trouble with lethal injections in recent months. In May, state officials halted the execution of Tony Carruthers when staff couldn’t get a secondary IV successfully placed after placing one IV into his right arm.

Later, the state’s execution of Anthony Darrell Hines was performed in August without any reported issues with placing the IVs, according to The Associated Press.

Advocates said issues with Tennessee’s procedures speak to larger issues around the death penalty.

“It’s not isolated to just one particular person or one particular execution team,” Kat Jutras, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Alternatives for Arizona, told CNN. “If we look at it in that very microlens, we’re not seeing the broader picture with the death penalty itself and lethal injections really being at the forefront of some of the larger problems.”

Pike, who along with her boyfriend was convicted for the 1995 torture and killing of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, was one of the youngest women sent to death row.

During her scheduled execution Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, executioners struggled to set the IV lines necessary to administer the lethal dose of pentobarbital. Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, told reporters she cooperated with the execution team and tried to give them tips on how to insert the IV lines, as she had warned the state she had a history with difficult vein access.

But her lawyers said issues with the IV resulted in the barbiturate, which slows the central nervous system, flowing into her body instead of her bloodstream. After the first dose failed to work, executioners administered a second dose.

“We may never know what sort of torture she endured during that process,” Ferrell, an assistant federal defender in Tennessee, said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” It’s unclear whether she was conscious or in physical pain during the procedure and subsequent life-saving treatment, he added.

“We don’t know what the prognosis is, as in the long-term prognosis, if she recovers,” he said, saying she remained unconscious in the hospital as of Sunday morning. “She may not fully recover.”

Her lawyers have called on the governor to commute Pike’s death sentence. After being convicted of first-degree murder, Pike has served more than 30 years in prison, mostly in solitary confinement, only to be brought out for a failed execution, Ferrell said.

“This has been a serious punishment for a very serious and awful crime,” Ferrell said. “I don’t think that attempting another execution is going to bring justice.”

The state Attorney General’s Office hasn’t given an indication of whether they’ll seek to put her to death again, he added.

Gov. Lee, who is term-limited after serving for eight years, will leave office in January. Republican US Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is running to replace him, has called to bring back the electric chair to “deliver justice for these victims swiftly.”

Some Tennessee lawmakers, including state House Speaker Cameron Sexton, have also proposed allowing the firing squad as an alternative execution method. At least five states have authorized the use of a firing squad for the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, told CNN affiliate WTLV/First Coast News she believes the state failed her family, more than three decades after Pike killed Slemmer, who was 19.

“I think the state owes me a big apology,” she said.

Traveling from Florida with her husband, Martinez spent hours at the Nashville-area prison waiting to see Pike’s execution. But the curtains eventually closed in the execution area and witnesses had to leave. They were later told Pike was being taken to the hospital, Martinez said.

Martinez said she worries about Pike being out and said her family hasn’t been told whether her daughter’s murderer will return to prison.

“All I wanted was justice,” she said.

Now she, along with state officials, must wait for answers to lingering questions of what went wrong with the execution and what’s next for Pike.

CNN’s Dakin Andone, Eric Levenson, Lauren del Valle and Ryan Young contributed to this report.

title: Soldiers and Gold Star families press Army leadership after deadly Iranian drone strike
