fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — On a sunny, cloudless morning on March 1, the day after President Donald Trump started the war against Iran, Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan was coordinating critical Army supplies out of Port Shuaiba in Kuwait.

In an instant, a drone crashed through the ceiling and exploded, killing Marzan, who had served in the military for 36 years. The force flung soldiers into the air, fragments of sheet metal and glass shards impaling them. The tin roof was peeled back "like opening up a sardine can," one soldier recalled.

Six soldiers were killed and dozens were injured in the deadliest known strike on U.S. troops since Operation Epic Fury commenced on Feb. 28.

For many, the attack at Port Shuaiba has receded into memory as the war nears its eighth month. But to those there that day and their families, it showed the cost of a hastily drawn conflict. The planning had apparent flaws, and commanders did not take intelligence reports of the Iranian threat seriously enough, leaving wounded soldiers questioning Army leadership and the military medical system.

In the aftermath, many of the wounded — some with decades of service and combat experience — told The Associated Press that commanders had been warned that the facility, a rectangular building with wooden sides at a working seaport and industrial area south of Kuwait City, was particularly vulnerable to a drone strike.

That warning went unheeded, the soldiers say. Some also said higher-ranking officers pushed for an all-clear to be called, but it's not certain from their accounts who ultimately made the decision to move soldiers out of a safer space in nearby bunkers. The wounded also would later say their serious injuries were not treated promptly or adequately in the weeks following the attack.

"We have the right to know what really happened," Marzan's widow, Tina Marzan, told the AP. "If somebody messed up, those people need to be held responsible."

Battlefield conditions are inherently chaotic and assessments drawn by those involved are often in tension. The AP's account of the attack is based on interviews with 13 soldiers, primarily officers, serving in key positions of responsibility there or familiar with high-level briefings leading up to the strike.

Along with several Gold Star families — the military's designation for relatives of a soldier killed while on active duty — many are raising their concerns publicly for the first time and calling for the Army to reconcile what they say are failures of preparedness.

Several soldiers spoke on the record, which is rare for troops still in the Army. Others spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. Some details of the attack have been reported by other news organizations, including The Washington Post and CBS News, but the AP is reporting other details for the first time.

In the early days of the war, Trump described it as a "little excursion" that would end quickly but now has no off-ramp in sight. The toll can be measured in 19 U.S. personnel killed, more than 800 wounded and at least $44 billion spent to wage the fight.

The Army declined to comment on the AP's reporting on the Port Shuaiba strike, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack. The Pentagon also declined to comment.

"Out of respect for the primary next of kin who will be scheduled for briefs on the official findings of the completed investigation, we will not comment on specific details, individual accounts, or leaked portions of the report at this time," the Army said in a statement.

The Army completed its investigation of the Port Shuaiba attack in June but has yet to release a report, citing the need to redact sensitive information, said an official familiar with the Army's investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the report has not been released.

The story of the attack really begins in June 2025, when the U.S. bombed three nuclear sites in Iran. In anticipation of a counterstrike on U.S. troops in Kuwait, military planners relocated soldiers to Port Shuaiba, which the Army used for decades on the belief it was safer.

In the lead-up to the war in February, that was the same playbook followed by Major Gen. John Hinson, the two-star general overseeing logistics for U.S. Central Command in the Middle East, and Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who led the 103rd Expeditionary Sustainment Command, an Iowa-based Army Reserve unit serving a nine-month deployment in Kuwait under Hinson's command. All six soldiers who died, and many of the dozens wounded, were from the 103rd.

Hinson and Barnes chose not to deviate from the plan despite knowing that the port lacked defenses against drones and was seen as increasingly likely to be attacked, according to five officers and an enlisted soldier familiar with the U.S. intelligence and threat assessments. The generals were following orders made at U.S. Army Central, which oversees Army units in the Middle East, and Central Command to leave the nearby Army base, Camp Arifjan.

Hinson declined to comment on the record for this story. Barnes did not respond to text messages and telephone calls.

Even before the attack, the threat of a drone strike was well known. But the command team rejected proposals to move the entire logistics headquarters to other sites identified as safer locations outside Kuwait, farther away from Iran, according to Major Billy Key, an operations planner working for Barnes who has served in the Army for more than 20 years. Another officer confirmed the alternate plans were scuttled. The port was about 65 miles (104 kilometers) from the Iranian border.

"Kuwait was just too close, that's the bottom line," Key said. "Kuwait was in striking distance of low-flying drones."

Senior leadership believed that a core group of the more than 200 soldiers who had been handling logistics at Camp Arifjan needed to remain in Kuwait. Two senior officers, including Lt. Col. Tim Halbur, told the AP that there were communications advantages to being there, so a small crew of about 75 soldiers was sent to the port to set up a temporary field headquarters for logistics in the region. Dozens of troops from other units were also present.

One enlisted soldier, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the command team is facing unfair criticism for hard decisions to balance its ability to carry out a crucial logistics mission with the inherent risks of war.

But six officers told the AP that the logistics headquarters' jobs could have been done from a safer site outside Kuwait, so long as they had access to a secure communications network.

"We did our work on a computer," Key told the AP. "We could have been anywhere."

During meetings, officers overseeing protection told Hinson and Barnes, among others, that Port Shuaiba would not be safe for troops due to the lack of air protection against drones, according to five soldiers who were present: Key, Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom and three others familiar with high-level briefings who insisted on anonymity due to fear of reprisal.

They said the generals were more focused on defending against missiles and were not prepared for drone warfare. "This type of fight has been going on for five years in Ukraine, and our excuse is we didn't expect it to happen to us," Ramsbottom said. "That's preposterous in my mind."

While the three major U.S. military bases in Kuwait had bolstered air protection heading into the war, the only U.S. air support for Port Shuaiba came from a Patriot anti-missile system in the vicinity of Camp Arifjan that was ill-equipped for shooting down Iranian drones.

While the system is capable of detecting the small aircraft, large numbers of drones are able to quickly deplete a battery, and the Patriot missiles cost vastly more than the drones. Using the system to down drones also then leaves the area vulnerable to far more deadly missile attacks.

Neither Hinson nor Barnes was empowered to change anti-air or drone defenses at the site.

"There was nothing that was going to intercept a threat coming at us other than ballistic missiles," Ramsbottom said.

Just days before the relocation to the port in late February, a group of intelligence officers pressed Hinson and Barnes to not go there. Hinson asked whether Port Shuaiba was on a list of planned Iranian targets that had been obtained by U.S. intelligence before Operation Epic Fury and was told that it was not on the list but was considered a likely secondary target, according to two officers familiar with the meeting.

The officers said Hinson still made the call to go.

Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank, then leading Army Central, signed off on the plan to move to Port Shuaiba when Hinson briefed him, Halbur and another senior officer said.

"Obviously, somewhere at the two-star, three-star level, they knew the intelligence reports," Halbur said. "We were just told, like, 'Hey, yeah, we'll be fine there.'"

One officer who was involved in logistics and was wounded in the attack said staying at the Kuwaiti port seemed appropriate. Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón of the Defense Logistics Agency said Port Shuaiba had existing infrastructure for secure communications that could accommodate their unit and Jordan, where U.S. military operations also are based and many soldiers were being relocated, was already getting crowded.

At the start of the war, missiles from all sides lit up the screen inside the command post at the port. Soldiers rushed in and out of bunkers. They could feel booms shake the ground.

That night, at least five quadcopter drones hovered over the port and appeared to be surveilling the U.S. military site, according to Key, who said one was only about 40 feet (12 meters) above him. He said he told senior officers what he saw, and it was passed up the chain. "That was the last I heard about it," he added. Intelligence briefings had warned that quadcopter drones were a sign of impending strikes.

The next morning, March 1, Capt. Cody Khork, who oversaw safety for the unit and had strongly advised against going to the port, confided to Ramsbottom that he felt they should not leave their bunker because of the barrage of missiles and drones coming in, according to Ramsbottom. Both Khork and Ramsbottom were concerned that the radar being used to issue all-clears was not picking up low-flying drones.

"We knew we were not safe," said Ramsbottom, who would end up with a piece of shrapnel sticking out of his head and a traumatic brain injury. "No one knew the drone situation."

In the hours before the deadly strike, higher-ranking officers pushed Khork to get troops cleared to leave the bunkers, said Ramsbottom, who was with Khork in the bunker. The team was under tremendous pressure to carry out its mission, which included tracking munitions levels and fuel across the region, and that could not be done from inside the bunker.

It remains unclear who ultimately made the decision to leave the bunkers, which were within several hundred feet of the operations center. Around 10 a.m., about 20 minutes after the final all-clear was issued, an Iranian drone smashed through the operation center's roof.

Ramsbottom and Key recalled the drone struck seconds after Khork passed by them and said "good morning." Key was blasted into a metal cabinet and knocked unconscious. When he awoke, his ears were ringing and he stumbled through the rubble, coming across Khork's lifeless body. A group of soldiers helped take Khork's body from the wreckage to ensure he could be buried with dignity.

Key later recounted the scene to Khork's parents at his funeral in Florida several weeks later, telling them their son appeared to die instantly.

"I would have wanted someone to tell my family that if it were me," Key said. "I felt compelled to tell them exactly what happened."

Lincón, a West Point graduate, remained conscious but was severely wounded by shrapnel and briefly lost his eyesight. Another wounded soldier bandaged him and got him out of the burning building.

"Had it not been for those brave souls, there would have been a lot more, including myself, who probably (would have) burned there in place," Lincón said.

Hinson and Barnes also suffered traumatic brain injuries from the blast, and Hinson's hand was hit with shrapnel.

The soldiers based at Port Shuaiba headed into war without having implemented a broad-based plan for a mass casualty event, seven soldiers, including senior officers stationed there, told the AP. Soldiers who still had their phones intact used Google to locate the nearest medical facilities. Some among the wounded would later say their serious injuries were not treated promptly or adequately in the weeks after the strike.

A medical service officer had prepared an evacuation plan that would have included setting up collection points for transporting wounded soldiers, but she was among the group sent to Jordan, and her plan was never briefed and put into place. She declined to comment.

"I've been in Iraq and Afghanistan. I've been in combat operations before. I know what right looks like, and this was not right by any means," said Chief Warrant Officer 4 Jonathan Tenbrink, who has spent 35 years in the U.S. military and was wounded by shrapnel in his forehead, face, neck, shoulders and right arm.

Relocating to Port Shuaiba, some soldiers acknowledged there was also a false sense of security.

"It was the farthest thing from my mind that we would get hit there," said Lincón, who had deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan multiple times in his 27-year Army career.

Even for survivors, there was peril ahead.

Halbur had been among a group of about nine soldiers medically evacuated, and he was having surgery at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland within a week, describing his care there as "excellent." He said he was told by visiting top Army leadership that the Port Shuaiba soldiers were "the guinea pigs" for the medical system as Operation Epic Fury commenced.

But other wounded soldiers, including those with serious head injuries and shrapnel wounds, had vastly different experiences of delayed care after the attack.

One group, some of whom were treated at a Kuwaiti hospital for about 48 hours, holed up in residential homes in Kuwait for another week as Iran unleashed missiles and drones that made it risky for evacuation flights. Soldiers finally boarded a cargo plane flown to Germany.

There, they say, they were not admitted to inpatient care at the military's main medical hub, the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center, but were sent to Army barracks because they had not been documented as combat-injured troops. About a week later they were placed into demobilization at Fort Hood in Texas, a process not focused on providing medical care.

A Pentagon official told the AP that Landstuhl's mission is to stabilize patients to transfer them for specialized care at a military hospital in the U.S., rather than admit them. In a statement, the Pentagon said that all wounded troops who arrive at its medical facilities are evaluated and may be admitted based on the severity of the injury.

In early July, Gold Star families received a briefing from Frank, who had just ended his rotation as head of Army Central Command, providing a broad overview of the investigation's findings. Tina Marzan said there was no admission of error.

Frank did not say anything about Port Shuaiba's vulnerabilities, only that soldiers were moved around because attacks on other bases were expected, according to Marzan. Frank also told her that there was proper medical treatment available to those at Port Shuaiba, she said.

"Whatever happened unfortunately does not bring my husband back," Marzan said.

One senior officer filed a complaint against Barnes and Hinson to the Army's inspector general. But in a July 20 letter reviewed by the AP, the watchdog concluded that Barnes had not engaged in misconduct or "ignored reliable intelligence" in this complaint based on "the limited evidence" provided by the officer.

The agency also noted this complaint against Hinson was withdrawn, which the officer disputed to the AP. The officer told the AP he relayed his conversations with Barnes discussing intelligence briefings but told investigators he had not directly interacted with Hinson.

Halbur, a father of two from Ankeny, Iowa, had been deployed as an Army reservist seven months earlier, hardly expecting to be on the front lines of a full-blown conflict.

He had served for nearly 30 years, but today he can no longer salute. His dominant right arm will likely never be able to bend past 90 degrees again after the blast shattered his forearm in four places, including his elbow.

"I can't squeeze both arms around my kids because my one arm won't allow me to do that anymore," Halbur said. "I want to coach my son's football team, but at the same time, I can't show them how to throw a football."

He says that his children, age 7 and 8, are coming to learn that "dad's never going to be the same."

He wears the names of the six soldiers who died at Port Shuaiba engraved in a metal wristband: Maj. Cody Khork, 35, an easygoing history buff; Master Sgt. Noah L. Tietjens, 42, a passionate martial arts instructor; Maj. Jeffrey R. O'Brien, 45, a father of three who loved playing the saxophone; Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor, a 39-year-old mother of two with a knack for sarcasm; 20-year-old Sgt. Declan J. Coady, an avid outdoorsman and Eagle Scout; and Marzan, 54, a mentor to many younger soldiers. Khork, Tietjens, Amor and Coady received posthumous promotions.

Halbur said that he looks at the wristband whenever he feels depressed by his arm's limitations.

"I know that there are six families who would give that up in a heartbeat," he said. "So that always kind of gives me a little more motivation to not be so glum about the things that I can't do in my future. I'm still here." ___ Brook reported from New Orleans, Watson from San Diego and Bynum from Savannah, Ga. Associated Press journalists Nicholas Ingram in Ankeny, Iowa, and Thomas Peipert in Colorado Springs, Colo., contributed to this report.

title: Student gave Cornell police leads in alleged rape and thought it was ‘in good hands’
description:
Jane Doe’s lawsuit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell University and the DA’s handling of her allegations.   (Heather Ainsworth for NBC News)
A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case.  
The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20.
fullText:
A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case.

The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20.

The student recalled rumors that Doe was planning to have a threesome but that it had “gone off the rails,” and she remembers being “really horrified by it.”

“From that night, I think, we just kind of started, like, hearing more,” the student said.

Talk of the alleged sexual assault became widespread on campus after the school issued a crime safety alert about a report of a sexual assault at a fraternity.

“The thing I think we all feel, like, betrayed in regards to is that, like, it wasn’t handled,” she said. “When we got the police report, I think we all assumed it was being, you know, it would be, like, handled properly, yeah, and it was, like, in good hands.”

The student, who discussed details corroborated by documents reviewed by NBC News, said she and a friend initially gave a tip to authorities after the crime alert was issued. Police later called her and asked her to come in and speak with them days after Doe reported the incident to Cornell police on Nov. 8.

The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because “it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl.” Doe’s lawsuit included a screenshot of a Chi Phi Snapchat group message that said there was “free p----” in a room in the frat house where Doe was the night she alleges she was assaulted.

“That was, like, when I kind of internally made the decision. OK, like, I’m taking this all in, and then I’m going to the police tomorrow,” the student said.

She recalled sitting with one or two officers for about half an hour during her interview with police.

“They seemed fairly competent. It seemed like a normal interview process to me,” she said.

She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of that evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she is familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept.

“I guess I assumed that, like, I wasn’t enough,” the student said.

Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday on the student’s account to police. In a video statement Saturday, President Michael I. Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” and said they raise questions about the investigations that were conducted. He said he welcomes an independent review of how the university handled the matter, which will be conducted by an outside law firm.

Police records obtained by NBC News showed that Cornell police spoke to multiple witnesses and fielded anonymous tips about the allegations of a gang rape at the fraternity house — but that the information was not referred to the local prosecutor for review in his deciding whether to bring charges.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NBC News on Friday that the interviews that were flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.” He did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.

Van Houten ultimately determined the allegations did not warrant charges because of a lack of criminality.

Doe’s suit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell and Van Houten’s handling of her allegations. Van Houten has since agreed to reopen his inquiry into Doe’s allegations, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the matter.

The student who spoke with campus police criticized how the department handled the matter. While students believed there was an active investigation into Doe’s claims, people continued going to Chi Phi, including the room at the center of the allegations.

Within Greek life at Cornell, “rumors spread fast,” the student said, and even if you did not know Doe or the men, “you knew someone who did.”

Doe’s lawsuit named Cornell, Chi Phi and the seven fraternity brothers among the defendants. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.

Cornell said in a statement on Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions” from the university.

According to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation, two of the fraternity members were expelled, and another two were suspected. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and “reflection papers.”

Attorneys for two of the seven men have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the five other men.

Chi Phi’s national fraternity condemned sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in a statement Wednesday. It said that the fraternity members Doe named were kicked out of the organization and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter.

“At every level of Chi Phi, we will take steps like these whenever they are needed to protect the integrity of our fraternity and the safety of our communities,” said Trey Robb, the national fraternity’s interim executive director.

Some of the men faced backlash as talk spread on campus.

Two of the Chi Phi brothers named in the suit were kicked out of their rugby club after the allegations came to light, a former teammate told NBC News.

“We kicked [them] off the team immediately before the school expelled them,” said the teammate, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.

The teammate said he has participated in discussions among a group of current and former rugby players about responding publicly to Doe’s lawsuit.

“As a team, it was important for us to support this victim,” he said. “We are extremely, extremely distraught.”

Cornell Rugby said in a statement that it was “deeply disturbed” by the allegations and that its thoughts were with Doe.

“Players who were known to be connected with the alleged events were permanently removed from the team and alumni network as soon as their affiliation with the incident was established,” it said.

No current members of the team have been affiliated with Chi Phi, the statement said.

As news of the allegations spread, some discussions were supportive of Doe, but others shamed her in conversations, a former member of Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta, told NBC News.

“Some people were sympathizing with Jane Doe, but also, people didn’t know details,” said the former member, who has graduated and requested anonymity out of a concern for privacy.

Another student and former member of Tri Delta told NBC News that she recalled learning about the incident through rumors and described the student body as “really pissed off about it.”

That student said that she was at the same sorority-hosted event the evening of Oct. 19 that Doe attended and which was referred to in her lawsuit but that Doe disappeared during the evening.

A few days later, the student said, Doe said people were spreading rumors about her and she was not sure what to make of it, “and it just seemed like everybody was very confused at the moment.”

A third former Tri Delta member told NBC News that the campus learned of the incident from the university alert and described students feeling “shock” and “really appalled.”

She, too, is critical of how Cornell handled the matter.

“I think that shows a lack of respect for their female students and kind of makes it less enticing to attend the university,” she said.

Today, within the sorority there is a resounding wave of support for Doe, she said, as well as “frustration and anger.”

Tri Delta said in a statement on behalf of its national organization and its Cornell chapter, “As an organization, we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

title: Sam Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening’ for benefits of AI
description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman admits "something's clearly not working" with the artificial intelligence money that has flooded the midterm elections — and he doesn't expect President Donald Trump's rebrand of the technology to improve his industry's image with the American public, either.
"I get why AI has a really negative perception right now," Altman told Brendan Bordelon in an exclusive interview marking the launch of Decoded by POLITICO. "I don't think spending money on politics is what's going to make people feel better about it. The industry needs to figure out a way to address what the actual concerns are, and right now, a lot of people in the industry are being quite tone deaf."
In the wide-ranging conversation, Altman offered a window into how OpenAI is confronting new political pressures and intensified competition with Anthropic, its corporate archrival run by former employee Dario Amodei.
fullText:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman admits "something's clearly not working" with the artificial intelligence money that has flooded the midterm elections — and he doesn't expect President Donald Trump's rebrand of the technology to improve his industry's image with the American public, either.

"I get why AI has a really negative perception right now," Altman told Brendan Bordelon in an exclusive interview marking the launch of Decoded by POLITICO. "I don't think spending money on politics is what's going to make people feel better about it. The industry needs to figure out a way to address what the actual concerns are, and right now, a lot of people in the industry are being quite tone deaf."

In the wide-ranging conversation, Altman offered a window into how OpenAI is confronting new political pressures and intensified competition with Anthropic, its corporate archrival run by former employee Dario Amodei.

Altman says OpenAI is more tolerant than Anthropic of less-than-catastrophic harms from AI, drawing out what he sees as a fundamental split in worldview between the two leading labs even as they converge on tougher rules in the wake of high-profile autonomous hacking incidents.

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," said Altman, who characterized those harms as linked to "the lighter touch regulatory stance that we advocate for."

"I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff."

The OpenAI head also suggested there needs to be a new "liability framework" for companies whose models are capable of autonomous cyberattacks, like the Hugging Face hack over the summer and incidents involving government websites. Altman called that behavior "clearly unacceptable," and said that "if something goes wrong with our models during training, there's going to be some version of that we need to be responsible for."

"This is the kind of thing that we are hoping our policymakers will all debate," he added, as Congress remains deadlocked.

And while Altman defended a "morally binding" AI safety accord that Trump signed with tech CEOs last week as a great start for the industry, he predicted calls for guardrails will continue and said he would "welcome something more." He also said he shares the concerns of those who worry AI rules are being crafted by the White House and tech executives without input from Congress or the public.

"If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong," Altman said.

Trump paired last week's AI agreement with an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to "super intelligence." It's a term Altman considers more accurate, though he doubts the public will find it "less scary." He expects people to keep using "AI" — and unlike Elon Musk, he won't be renaming OpenAI to OpenSI. "Brands are sticky," Altman said.

Throughout the interview, Altman sought to explain his company's new policy posture. He recently agreed with Amodei on the need to slow down AI's development, and his lobbyists have increasingly followed Anthropic in backing new safety requirements at all levels of government.

But despite emphasizing "a lot of daylight" between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman also tried to distance himself — on both policy and politics — from the Silicon Valley investors who are spending heavily to block strict regulations, including through the pro-AI super PAC network Leading the Future.

"When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control to AI … this is where I would say to the accelerationists, let's be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future," he said, using a descriptor often applied to the tech leaders and advisers who have Trump's ear on AI.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman has pulled away from those donors as well, reportedly backing out of a second $25 million donation to LTF and apologizing to employees internally for creating a "distraction." (Altman said he hadn't seen The New York Times report when asked if he agreed that the money was counterproductive, and that LTF never approached him for money.)

From the AI race with China to his favorite world leader and why the ChatGPT maker hasn't made all of its hacks public, Altman went deeper with Decoded than we've heard him go before.

Read the full Decoded newsletter for more.

Also check out the full interview on YouTube and listen to the podcast here.

title: Flydubai co-pilot planned attack before airline hired him, Israeli officials say
description:
The flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain in a suspected attempt to crash the plane has told UAE interrogators he planned the attack before he was hired by the Dubai state-owned airline, according to two Israeli ‌officials with knowledge of the probe. 
   A third source briefed on the UAE probe said the co-pilot, an Omani national, had planned to crash ‌last Wednesday's flight into Ben-Gurion airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but opted not ​to, the source added. 
   It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although the co-pilot is thought to have known someone onboard, the source said. 
   All of the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation.
fullText:
JERUSALEM, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain in a suspected attempt to crash the plane has told UAE interrogators he planned the attack before he was hired by the Dubai state-owned airline, according to two Israeli ‌officials with knowledge of the probe.

A third source briefed on the UAE probe said the co-pilot, an Omani national, had planned to crash ‌last Wednesday's flight into Ben-Gurion airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but opted not ​to, the source added.

It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although the co-pilot is thought to have known someone onboard, the source said.

All of the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did flydubai.

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, which had been bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general ‌has said, calling the incident a "terrorist attack".

Two sources have ⁠said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. Israeli officials have not named the co-pilot but have said he is from Oman. UAE authorities and flydubai have not publicly disclosed the co-pilot's identity.

INDIAN PILOT HAILED AS HERO FOR HELPING TO FOIL PLOT

The two Israeli officials said the co-pilot told interrogators that he had applied for a ​job ​at Dubai state-owned flydubai after searching for airlines that fly to Tel Aviv.

The third source ​said Israel was being continuously updated about the investigation from the ‌UAE.

Disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot. The pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, survived the attack and has been hailed as a hero for managing to open the cockpit door. The plane was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israeli.

A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred to the UAE on Thursday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said pilots who are citizens of countries that Israel does not have diplomatic ‌relations with, including Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is not ​clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the Tel Aviv flight, and Netanyahu has ​since ordered a security review of foreign airlines flying to Israel.

SUSPECT SPENT ​TIME IN NEW ZEALAND AS WELL AS AUSTRALIA

New Zealand Assistant Police Commissioner Michael Johnson said on Monday that the co-pilot had ‌spent time in the country and that NZ police were looking ​into the period. He did not say ​when the co-pilot allegedly visited the country or name him.

A multi-agency Australian counterterrorism unit is also investigating links to Australia of the co-pilot, who was once enrolled at RMIT University in Melbourne, Victoria. A fourth source said the co-pilot had studied there around a decade ago.

Netanyahu has said the ​co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly ‌suicidal, although he has not said when or where that indoctrination allegedly occurred. The co-pilot completed three months of theoretical training at Royal ​Air Maroc in 2025 but his application to work there was later rejected, according to the Moroccan airline.

title: U.S. removes B-1 bombers from U.K. air base after new security threat
description:
A Rockwell B1 Lancer heavy bomber takes off from RAF Fairford in Fairford, United Kingdom, on October 04. - David Bown/Getty Images
The United States has moved long-range bombers back to their American home stations after an unspecified new threat, according to a US official, days after the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the planes had been stationed.
“We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the official told CNN.
fullText:
The United States moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases on Sunday after an unspecified new threat, according to a US official. It comes days after the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the planes had been stationed.

“We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the official told CNN. The statement did not include details on why the planes were moved.

The source familiar called the latest threat a “real world incident.” It is unusual that the US military would move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official said.

A Downing Street spokesperson said that the UK government would not comment on foreign nations’ military operations. Asked about safety concerns by residents living near the base, the spokesperson told reporters that the UK has “the tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country, but not just that, throughout the world.”

The UK Ministry of Defense also declined to comment on the operations or capabilities of other nations.

The Royal Air Force base at Fairford has been used to deploy US B-1 bombers involved in the war against Iran and is an operating location for US Global Strike Command, which is tasked with managing long-distance strikes.

CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas said it was likely several dozen bombers were stationed at Fairford, adding that it was unusual to move all the aircraft.

“It speaks to the credibility and the seriousness of the threat overall to the base that we’re talking about,” he told Ben Hunte on CNN Newsroom.

The relocation of the bombers comes amid the investigation into the alleged plot. British police on September 27 arrested five men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses close to the airbase.

The men – identified only as British nationals between the ages of 23 and 25 and from the London area – were quickly released on bail, with police confirming no explosives were found in three vans at the scene. Their release sparked criticism from President Donald Trump, who said “I wouldn’t have done that.”

A 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was also arrested on Thursday in connection with the alleged plot.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the incident.

“We will say 

Burnham’s remarks appeared to support the US’ assessment that the incident involved a foreign actor. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said “the hands of a foreign actor” were involved in the alleged plot but declined to provide details in an interview with Fox News last week.

“I think it ties us to the reality here. We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said.

Meanwhile, Iran has denied any involvement in the incident, described the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran, Iranian state media reported Thursday. During the meeting, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Majid Takht-Ravanchi reportedly urged London to revise what he called its “inappropriate approach” toward Tehran.

This has been updated with additional details.

CNN’s Nic Robertson, Max Saltman, Chandler Thornton Tim Lister and James Frater contributed to this report.

title: My New Course at UT Austin: AI Alignment Theory
description: This semester, I’ve been teaching a brand-new course, entitled CS395T AI Alignment Theory. Here’s the course description: The astounding progress of AI over the past decade has been acc…
fullText:
This semester, I’ve been teaching a brand-new course, entitled CS395T AI Alignment Theory. Here’s the course description:

The astounding progress of AI over the past decade has been accompanied by a rising fear: do we really understand how to align and control powerful AI systems—how to get them reliably to do what we wanted, or would want them to do on reflection, rather than merely what we said? If we succeed at building general-purpose superhuman intelligences along the current paradigm, should we expect that development to go well for humanity? Can we modify the design, training, monitoring, or scaffolding of those intelligences to help ensure that it goes well? While there’s been a great deal of recent empirical work touching on these questions, this course will concentrate mainly on theoretical and mathematical foundations. As a warning, the theoretical foundations of AI alignment have not yet gelled into any one coherent body of results accepted as canonical by the field. Nevertheless, in this course, we’ll read and debate many of the conceptual and mathematical works that have been most influential in the AI alignment field, from both before and during the current LLM revolution. Student presentations, reports, and projects will play a central role.

I vividly remember encountering Eliezer Yudkowsky and his Sequences 20 years ago. I remember thinking: even if these people talk and act like crazy cultists, still, let me bend over backwards to be epistemically virtuous, and entertain their ideas on their merits, as very few academics would. Even if, of course, I ultimately end up rejecting the ideas, on the simple ground that powerful AI is such an absurdly remote prospect that it’s almost impossible to say anything useful about it today, outside the realm of speculative fiction.

For my failure to see what was coming, it seems like an appropriate punishment that I’m now, in 2026, effectively teaching a course on Yudkowsky Studies. And it’s the most important course I can teach.

Well, for some definition of “teach.” The thing about AI alignment is that there’s no textbook (though apparently ILIAD is working on one), no core of nontrivial theorems considered canonical by the field, no real body of mathematical theory at all. This makes it extremely different from the courses I’m used to teaching, like Quantum Information Science or Computability and Complexity.

So we’ve been running the course as a discussion seminar. Every session, a “rapporteur” presents an AI alignment research paper or other reading; then I and others ask questions and discuss. Some of the readings (like Omohundro on the “basic AI drives,” or Hadfield-Menell et al. on the off-switch game) predate the current LLM revolution, while others (like the METR report on the HuggingFace incident or Dario Amodei’s “We Must Pace the Frontier”) are so timely that they were only released while the course was underway. Most are somewhere in between.

I expected to have to make a case to students about why AI alignment is a pressing concern, why it’s no longer science fiction, etc. There was huge demand for the course, and while of course there’s a selection effect, the students who’ve shown up have been extremely engaged, sometimes criticizing the assigned papers for not taking existential risk seriously enough.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we didn’t get that criticism about our very first assigned reading, which was Eliezer Yudkowsky’s 2022 essay AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities—one the most canonical statements of what Eliezer believes and why that’s shorter than a book. Which brings me to the topic of the rest of this post! Our rapporteurs are not merely presenting the papers in class; they’re also submitting written reports about what the papers said, what their own thoughts were, and what were the highlights of the class discussion. And, with student permission, I’ll be sharing those reports on this blog!

So, without further ado, I present to you our first report, on Eliezer’s list of lethalities, by Tennyson Bardwell, who I thank for his work. Feel free to discuss in the comment section; some of the students might also chime in. Expect more reports here over the coming weeks.

UT Austin has a new Computer Science course this fall. Alongside familiar graduate-level classes such as Advanced Computer Networks and Convex Optimization sits CS 395T: AI Alignment Theory, taught by Scott Aaronson. This is one of a growing number of AI Alignment courses taught at academic institutions. Just as concerns over catastrophic consequences for misaligned AGI systems reach a broader public discourse, Eliezer Yudkowsky—one of the loudest voices in the field and author of the first assigned reading in Professor Aaronson’s course—is declaring the cause hopeless.

Thus, the students of AI Alignment Theory began their semester by reading a laundry list of critical problems in AI Alignment research, how failure to solve those problems will result in catastrophic consequences, and the reasons to be pessimistic about both past and future progress on these problems. The essay by Eliezer, titled AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities and posted to his popular community-driven website LessWrong in 2022, is divided into three sections.

Section A roughly describes the magnitude of the AI Alignment problem. That is, the magnitude of the consequences for a complete failure to align an AGI system to human values before construction. It posits that AGI would quickly catch up to all human knowledge simply by learning from existing human productions (colloquially referred to as “eating the internet”) and then, nearly as quickly, begin to meaningfully surpass human knowledge. AlphaGo Zero is presented as a model both for how this might happen, and how it might be difficult to correctly predict beforehand. Many believed that AlphaGo’s success in the board game Go was chiefly attributed to its ability to learn from the extensive history of human-played games. Less than a year after AlphaGo beat the best human player, the successor system AlphaGo Zero surpassed the original AlphaGo. Unlike its predecessor, AlphaGo Zero was trained in just three days by exclusively playing against itself without seeing a single human game.

This quick ramp from AGI to super-intelligence would pose a different sort of problem than humans are generally used to dealing with. Unlike traditional problems in science and engineering, the consequence for a failed attempt might not leave room for another try. An intelligent entity with a misaligned goal would be well aware that it stands in opposition to humans, and might act deceitfully until in a position to act openly against humans without jeopardizing its own survival. Since most goals benefit from control of power and resources, it seems likely that nearly any goal-driven intelligence would have ample opportunity to be misaligned with human desires.

Section B describes reasons why, by default, any AGI that humans build using current methods is likely to be unaligned even if considerable attention is paid to the topic. This “current method” is gradient descent. That is, incremental progress with respect to some loss function which “punishes” a model for undesirable behavior. A notoriously elusive property of such trained models is the ability to generalize out of their training distributions. To train a primitive model to be aligned to humans might involve learning a great many behavioral rules. However, the sorts of rules needed to keep a drastically smarter agent in check might not always be relevant to simpler models (e.g., “do not emotionally dysregulate humans you speak with” might not be relevant to a simpler model that is less able to reliably get under the skin of humans it operates with, or which is assigned tasks in training which do not benefit from such anti-social behavior).

Eliezer focuses on the misalignment of humans with their creators (evolution or evolutionary pressures) as a critical data point for reasoning about misaligned intelligent systems. Despite being a generally slow process, evolution eventually created a runaway intelligent system (Homo sapiens) which proceeded to dominate the globe, decimate related species, and eventually (it is forecasted) effectuate population decline. That last development is arguably in opposition to the sole imperative demanded by evolution: to reproduce.

Section B also makes time for criticism of the most popular paths toward AI alignment, including interpretability (unworkable, and attempting to train on it evokes Goodhart’s law, incentivizing deceit), using multiple AIs to maintain a balance of power (it is not clear how multiple strong AIs unaligned with humanity results in better outcomes for the weak humans), and corrigibility (it seems impossible to motivate an AI system to effect outcomes without also motivating it to desire its own survival to effectuate said outcomes).

Section C describes a bleak state of affairs in which veterans in AI alignment are unsatisfied with current progress and do not have a plan to deliver tangible solutions before the advent of AGI systems. In particular, Eliezer describes recent results as showy but useless. He believes that even with additional funding, the lack of appropriate evaluation mechanisms will prevent the most effective researchers from rising to the top.

A summary of the landscape, as described by Eliezer, in the flowchart below.

Figure 1: A flow chart of (select) paths described by Eliezer in his essay. A common feature of this flow chart is that many “good states”—such as disabling a misbehaving AGI or choosing not to build an AGI—are not “final” states in the sense that they are not permanent solutions. Such a state merely represent the avoidance of a single potential disaster, rather than the emergence of a new stable world state. Hence, these nodes posses back-arrows.

Despite the bleak content, Eliezer’s colorful prose inspired a lively class discussion. Before this discussion started, a survey was taken of the class’s predictions for various outcomes of the AGI in the coming years (with the full results below in figure 2). This survey asked students for their opinion of a number of statements. Each of these individual statement, if true, would reduce concerns of catastrophic AI-driven disasters. For example, when asked “How much do you agree with the statement: Humans will choose to not build AGI” half of respondents said they strongly disagreed with high confidence (agreement = 1, confidence = 5). Students also generally disagreed with the statements:

There was a divergence in responses regarding interpretability, corrigibility, and “other” AI alignment research. In the latter two cases, a plurality of respondents (about a quarter) agreed strongly with statements that such research would defang AGI (agreement = 4, confidence=4), while most other responses express various levels of agreement with low confidence. However, when asked about the likelihood of interpretability research defanging AI, the pessimistic voices were more united. A quarter of responses still expressed the same optimism, but roughly half expressed pessimism (agreement ≤ 2) with half of those expressing at least moderate confidence (confidence ≥ 4). Based on the following discussion, this might have been caused by more familiarity with interpretability research, including first-hand experience.

The only statement with general agreement was “(hyper-)AGI will understand human intentions better than we can code it.” However, it should be noted that no statement such as “AGI will respect human desires, as it understand them” was asked on the survey.

Figure 2: Class Survey Results; conducted before a class-wide discussion. Note that students were instructed to answer confidence = 1 when they had not previously considered the statement, to answer confidence = 3 when they felt there were strong arguments on both sides, and to answer confidence = 5 when they possessed well-considered resolve.

After the survey was completed, the results were displayed as an open discussion began. Similar to recent empirical research from frontier labs, interpretability research received more airtime than in Eliezer’s article. Students disagreed first about the definition of interpretability: whether it refers to the ability to interpret a model’s behavior solely by its weights, to interpration via repeated probing of the model in a sandbox, or whether it can also refer to the modern chain-of-thought traces. Regardless of how it was defined, however, participants were either pessimistic or very pessimistic about interpretability research broadly. One student criticized common misunderstandings of chain of thought. Rather than being a verbatim copy of the models internal dialog, it is instead a superficial summary of the complete thought state and routinely produced gibberish, such as rarely used Chinese characters in the middle of otherwise English reasoning.

A popular topic was the exact shape and speed of a recursive self-improvement loop. If it takes place slowly, then what might we learn from “near misses” such as the Hugging Face incident? The number of near misses we are able to learn from before AI possesses sufficient power to prevent further iterations could depend on this curve, with some students arguing that the sheer number of humans, as well as their default robustness in the physical world compared to AI systems means that AI-driven extinction events are still a long way off. Bolstering this “slow take-off” opinion are rumors that AI already plays a major role in model development which could be interpreted as the start of this process.

Some criticized a focus on “solving ethics” as a needlessly high bar that distracts from the more mundane tasks dominating AI alignment work. In particular, the student volunteer who presented this paper (and the author of this report) included a section on “Ethical Dilemmas” in their presentation. Among arguments against focusing on abstract moral philosophy, Professor Aaronson cites Eliezer to emphasize that any alignment at all is difficult, not just in morally gray cases:

When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

In response, I argue that some examination of everyday decisions with a critical lens—such as telling white lies to loved ones or consuming animal products—can help disabuse us of the notion that goodness emerges in every sufficiently intelligent agent.

One of the most interesting discussions was about the difference between state-of-the-art LLMs and the theorized AI agents long discussed in rationalist discourse. Since current LLMs “mimic the human distribution,” they come preloaded with extensive understanding of human social norms and moral behavior. This makes constitutional alignment (the current practices of using system prompts to establish ground rules) extremely effective. This might either fundamentally change the orthogonality thesis, or provide a new tool to better approximate human judgment in complicated situations.

Of all the points made, the one I found most interesting was simply (paraphrased):

I think human-alignment is just very tractable

Here, “human-alignment” refers not to AI alignment with human values, but cooperation between different humans. More specifically, it refers to the ability for human societies to choose not to rush recklessly into larger-and-larger AI systems. In an academic course focused on the technical problem of AI alignment, this was a reminder to not completely discard policy discussions in the believe that they lack any value. After all, many destructive technologies have been previously contained by international agreements. Notable examples include nuclear weapons and engineered plagues. However, even this was a contentious topic. The main criticisms were (1) the extreme “dual-use” nature of AIs for both peaceful growth and warfare, and (2) the greater danger for AI escapes even after taking precautions to prevent it. However, in the interest of ending on an optimistic note—unlike the assigned reading—it is on this belief in human cooperation that I will leave you.

title: Homestead: A framework around Claude Code
description: A year spent making Claude Code more useful: agents that coordinate, pick up requests as they arrive, and finish the work before it reaches me. By Joshua Mullet.
fullText:
The agents couldn’t talk to each other, so I played telephone between them.

Every agent got a walkie-talkie: it can see who else is working, what they’re on, and talk to them directly. One big project can now split across many agents that sort things out between themselves.

Nothing started until I copied a request over by hand.

I built an app that lets Claude Code read my notifications as they arrive. A text, an email, a Slack message — it sees the request before I do.

One agent doing everything did nothing well.

Alfred handles my notifications and only decides where each one goes. Every project has its own agent that knows exactly how I want that project run.

The work kept stopping at “mostly done.”

Each project is a Steading. A Worker does the job, and a Steward checks it against my standards and sends it back until every step is actually done — reproduced, fixed, proven, deployed, reply drafted.

Not where it is today. Where I’m taking it.

Some decisions only a person should make. The goal is one screen with you at the center: it hands you the next most important question, with the data you need to answer it right there. You decide, and everything else keeps moving.

Over time, more of the work can move to AI. Some of it never should. Homestead’s job is to take the busywork and leave you the decisions that are actually yours.

For it to know which question matters most, it has to understand my priorities and every channel the work comes through. That’s the hard part, and it’s what I’m building toward.

I don’t think anyone’s Homestead should look the same. And no one’s should ever be “done.” It should evolve with you.

A quick 15 minutes or a full hour — your call. Weekday mornings 8–9 and evenings 5–6, Eastern.

If these times don’t work, just email me and we can probably make something work.

Alfred is my AI assistant, not me. It answers questions about Homestead whenever you have them, so you don’t have to wait on me.

Hi — I'm Alfred, Joshua's assistant. Ask me anything about how Homestead works. Fair warning: I'm an AI, not Joshua.

Replies usually take a minute or two.

Everything Homestead runs on is open. Don’t try to set it up by hand, though. On its own it’s wired to my Mac, my phone and the way I work. Paste one prompt into Claude Code (or any agent) and it builds you your own, then helps you bend it to fit your work.

title: Refinement E-Graphs
description: The idea of a refinement e-graph is to add a baked in a <= relation that is about as privileged as the e-graph’s native =
fullText:
The idea of a refinement e-graph is to add a baked in a <= relation that is about as privileged as the e-graph’s native =

There is a story that compiler rewrites are often not bidirectional equalities, but instead are unidirectional refinement rewrites, moving from an abstract or floppy program / spec to a more completely determined one that can run on a concrete machine. It is quite common for the source language to be cagey about the exact order the children of an expression are evaluated, or what is the result of an integer overflow or division by zero. Being cagey may enable more optimization opportunities or ease translation to disparate machines. It is also just a fact of life for these languages.

Here is a prototype https://github.com/philzook58/refinement-microegg of a refinement egraph based on Max Willsey’s microegg https://github.com/mwillsey/microegg. A WASM demo is here https://www.philipzucker.com/refinement-microegg. Third verse same as the second

A nice example is “Don’t Care” in digital circuits https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don%27t-care_term , You may say that certain inputs are not supported to a circuit and that the result is a don’t care in that case. An optimizer is free to pick a result that allows for the most optimal circuit. I believe George Constantinides explained a version of this example to me.

There are also refinement rewrite rules available in the implementation, rewrite-le and rewrite-ge.

Spiritually, (rewrite-le lhs rhs) represents the formula forall ?a, lhs(?a) <= rhs(?a). Because of the form of this formula, we don’t have to match lhs on the equality nose. We can find a substitution for any starting ?t <= subst(lhs[?a]) to chain to a discovered inequality assertion ?t <= subst(lhs[?a]) <= subst(rhs[?a]).

I think semantics is really important and don’t like meaningless syntax manipulation. The intended semantics of this “Don’t Care” example is Bool -> Set Bool with <= representing pointwise set containment.

x could be generalized to have an algebra of more than one dimension, which would bring us back to lifting e-graphs https://www.philipzucker.com/lambda_miller_egg/ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h1CzZguA6DE . Refinement and Lambda afaik are orthogonal features that have no issue being bolted together. Maybe something interesting might occur in extraction (some related terms may not exist in some contexts)?

Note that this inequality assertion is distinct from equating dontcare = true = false. This of course is problematic. But it is also distinct from equating to either of them dontcare = true or dontcare = false. If we did one of these, then all dontcare everywhere would be forced to be true or false, whereas we want the ability to be able to make independent choices at all usages.
One could perhaps make dontcare1 dontcare2 dontcare3 etc as fresh constants and then independently equate them. This freshness game always feels like some goofy shell game to me though.
There is some intuitive sense that equating an eclass destroys it as a resource, but stating an inequality does not destroy it as a resource.

Roughly E-Graph = Union Find + Hash Cons. So a Refinement E-graph = inequality union find + hash cons.

The interface of the inequality union find is more important than the details of the implementation.

Previous discussions of mine on inequality union finds towards refinement e-graphs:

An (inequality) union find deals in atomic symbols e4 and atomic equations e5 = e87 (or inequations e4 <= e65).

An e-graph adds function symbols f(e4,e4) to this. These symbols appear in the following processes:

The e-graph implementation need to be told how the function symbols play with the inequality <= by the user. Functions always respect equality =, but they may be monotone, anti-monotone or neither/unknown in their individual arguments. I like set difference diff(A,B) as an example of this. It is monotone in the first argument but anti-monotone/contravariant in the second argument diff(+,-).

Instead of congruence closure, we can perform refinement closure. This basically is applying a theorems like forall a b c d, a <= b /\ c >= d -> diff(a,c) <= diff(b,d) instead of a = b /\ c = d -> diff(a,c) = diff(b, d) which is what congruence closure applies.

Refinement closure isn’t as nice as congruence closure. We can use it both in the form that makes new enodes or the form that only notes relations between pre-existing enodes. In a datalog sense, this is the difference between
diff(a,c) <= diff(b,d) :- a <= b, c >= d, diff(a,c) and the guarded version diff(a,c) <= diff(b,d) :- a <= b, c >= d, diff(a,c), diff(b,d). The first can be useful, but it can also be explosive.

Pattern matching can be modelled as a processing a constraint set {?p = t} (see for example section 2.2.3 of https://www.cs.bu.edu/fac/snyder/publications/UnifChapter.pdf or section 4.6 of Term Rewriting and All That ). What makes it pattern matching vs unification is having variable only on one side, which is sometimes easier/more efficient to implement.

For refinement e-matching, We can be working with a constraint {?p <= t} or {t <= ?p}. But otherwise really the algorithm doesn’t change that much. You just need to track which “mode” you’re currently in, and change the mode according to the variance of the function symbols.

For example, this diff pattern processes by flipping one of the modes.{diff(?a, ?b) <= diff(x,y)} ===> {?a <= x, ?b >= y}

In the implementation, there is one extra degree of nondeterminism on top of the usual e-matching eclass->enode nondeterminsm, where in the GE or LE mode, you may traverse an eclass -> eclass <= edge.

From the flattened relational e-matching perspective, this is the insertion of implicit (le ?a ?b) all throughout the pattern. For example the patternfoo(bar(?x)) becomes flattened to ?e1 = foo(?e2), ?e2 <= ?e3, ?e3 = bar(?e4), ?e4 <= ?x. <= kind of “mediates” between every function symbol relation.

Regular extraction is actually pretty similar to e-matching in many ways. We are seeking a ?extract = t but we want the “best” ?extract. We have a tendency to implement extraction bottom up instead of top down.

In refinement extraction, we can instead be asking for ?extract <= t or ?extract >= t. We might also want to use <= in our definition of “best”. Perhaps we want the most refined (which semantically might mean the most concretely implemented or most deterministic entity) and then tie break with smallest size term or vice versa.

This is basically a copy of my python microegg with some inequality smarts put in. There is a refinement closure step le_cong_step and le_cong_step_weak (which makes no new enodes). Because e-matching can traverse <= edges, you might need less materialization than you’d think.

ematching and extraction are keyed on Mode which says whether you are allowed to search up or down the <= or have to use on the nose =.

The variance table variance : dict[str, tuple[Variance, ...]] says the variance of each argument of the function symbol. It is kind of the same shape of data one might use for storying types of the symbols, but this implementation is untyped.

All told, I find refinement a shockingly simple extension of the usual egraph concepts and implementation. But it has felt mysterious before so maybe that means I’ve just become incredibly wise?

I think really the thing that makes it shockingly simple is just not believing there is any incredibly clever or nuanced way of doing it. I think the only way to do it is basically the obvious way.

I think that maybe the generalization of all this is an egraph rewriting system that supports multiple relations and annotations of how they push through function symbols, akin to https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V9.2.0/refman/addendum/generalized-rewriting.html

I remember being at a table at PLDI 2022 and Zach trying to convince / ask John Regehr what he wanted for e-graph to be compelling to him. He said refinement and as a treatment of arbitrary bitwidth bitvectors. These two have stuck with me as things to look for and this is the source of the refinement e-graph line of questioning.

I have debated rather than the mode + variance abstraction to allow specifying what expansion (EQ,GE,LE) you want in the language of the pattern. For example i could use (foo ?a), [foo ?a], {foo ?a} if I want to allow EQ, GE, LE respectively. This would allow fine grained ad hoc control of refinement e-matching in the pattern.

As Graham noted, the upper and lower sets of the Ids do fit operationally somewhat into the egg notion of Analyses. Generically, it makes perfect sense to have things keyed on Id that merge when Id merge. I am agnostic if that means such things must be Lattices (as many program analyses are), Semigroups (like eclass member counts) or something else. That the upper and lower sets themselves contain more Ids is fine but also defies a simple algebraic characterization of what is going on in my opinion.

There has been a similar debate if equality is “just a lattice of partitions”, trying to subsume the equality relation of the egraph into Lattices as the master concept. Didn’t seem to really work but operationally it kind of makes sense that equalities is implemented as a “merge action” very much akin to a lattice join at least operationally. There is spooky action at a distance through the union find though. Mutable references often enable some kind of spooky tunnelling phenomenon that break simple mathematical models https://counterexamples.org/polymorphic-references.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_restriction (Oleg Kiselyov had some way of casting types through a ref cell tunnel too?)

The mode extraction kind of says what kind of pattern we are procssing p <= t t <= p or t = p. Variance is a property of function symbols that says what we can infer about pushing <= through f. This is used in the upward direction for refinement closure, but in the downward direction for breaking apart a pattern matching constraint/query into queries on the arguments {f(?a, ?b) R f(x,y)} ===> {?a R x, ?b R y}. R may be flipped, kept the same, or forced to be equality because f isn’t known to be sufficiently monotone. It is always sound to revert an inequality query ?p <= t to equality ?p = t.

Extraction also comes in the same modes t = ?extract t <= ?extract t >= ?extract. Extraction is kind of similar to pattern matching in some respects

[[x]] = fun b => {b} is the lifted identity function. ite is pointwise lifted. [[dontcare]] = fun _ => {True, False} [[true]] = fun _ => {True} [[false]] = fun _ => {False}. Refinement is interpreted as subrelation.

I feel that for an abstract partial order relation, this is about as good as you’re going to do. I don’t think there is a some magic data structure that will make everything all better

But I do think there is the possibility to do better on two axes

A prototype of a refinement egraph based on Max Willsey’s microegg https://github.com/mwillsey/microegg. A WASM demo is here https://www.philipzucker.com/refinement-microegg

Refinement e-graphs give you an uninterpreted <= that is about as baked in as = is.

This is useful perhaps because as the story goes, many rewrites in compilers are not unoriented equalities, they are oriented refinements.

<= is baked in to be transitive, reflexive, and collapses cycles to =.

Previous discussions of mine on refinement e-graphs:

The union find tracks upper and lower <= sets in a manner similar to an analysis (they are keyed on eclass and merge on union). Tentatively, storing this maximally sparsely rather than fully materializing (DFSing it on demand) as one would in egglog is more performant in memory and time. Egglog itself is highly engineered though, so I don’t actually know how this shakes out.

A nice example is “don’t care” in boolean circuits . Some inputs are not expected or allowed, so they optimizer is free to pick a behavior on those inputs that helps make a more optimal circuit.

In either case, I think baking in <= rather than having it as a mangled program or macro is conceptually cohesive and pleasant.

Nothing involving <= is quite as well behaved or as performant as =, but it is there as a light sprinkling on top. If everything you do is refinement rather than equality, I am not sure the refinement egraph offers much over a hash cons with a stored inequality table.

E-matching, rebuilding, and extraction all have slight tweaks related to <=. Rebuilding performs refinement closure.

Function symbols can be given a variance signature, very similarly to variance of type parameters in subtyping. This is about whether they are monotone a <= b -> f a <= f b, anti-monotone a <= b -> f a >= f b or neither in particular arguments. This changes patterns and extraction “modes” appropriately as they go through the term.

Refinement rebuilding / closure is no where near as nice as equality (although it is still conceptually simple). It is not obvious that it will terminate if one allows new enode creation, so in that sense it is in the same naughty category as rewrite rules. There is a distinction to be made between materializing and non-materializing refinement closure (only note inequalities between pre-exising enodes).

You do sometimes want to enumerate your upper or lower set of ids for refinement closure, and for e-matching modulo refinement and extraction modulo refinement.

It is my belief that a completely generic uninterpreted refinement relation can never be as good as an equality relation and that there probably isn’t an astonishingly good way of implementing such a thing. It will more or less correspond to depth first search enumerations +- some tweaks.

Nevertheless, I think it is both nontrivial, interesting, and possibly useful to bake in an inequality relation into the surface language and features.

The alternative is to macro encode an inequality into something like egglog. I kind of prefer direct operational interpretations than a macro expansion explanation.

In small micro benchmarks it does appear that maintaining the sparse representation of the inequality relation with on the fly closure is superior to materializing it ahead of time in memory and speed (memory often implies speed since cache whatevers are a dominant concern).

Based on the results in https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1571066104002968 it is my suspicion that ground refinement closure may be undecidable. In this case, full refinement closure should be treated at the same level of suspicion and incompleteness as rules are.
